We've got one installed on the water gun and the other one installed on the spigot down in the LEB, and we - mention one problem with them is that they leak at the junction between the food bag and the water filter. speaker: CC
text: Roger. Sounds good. We'll check in on that problem with the SPAN guys and let you know in the morning. If you have to call us tonight, we'd like you to do it on DOWNVOICE BACKUP. We're configuring the MSFN for that mode; and as far as we can see, you're cleared for some z's. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Maybe we'll get around to lunch.

speaker: CC
text: How about a peanut butter and jelly?

text: Okay. I thought that was a - better way to clear the DSKY but evidently it isn't. Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: Apollo 11. ...

text: Okay, 11. This is Houston. speaker: LMP
text: Stand by.

speaker: LMP

text: Okay. Right now it reads, "To exit G&N PTC," then you've got a pen-and-ink change that says, "AUTO RCS SELECT, 12 MAIN A and B." And you come down to the printed step 1. speaker: LMP
text: Roger. I copy. Is that AUTO RCS SELECT, 12 MAIN A, MAIN B to be the ...

speaker: CC
text: Roger. It should be the second step in that procedure. At time 22 40, or when you get to it, we'd like to commence a charge on battery A. And at time 24 10, we have an updated attitude for your P52 and optics calibration. Over.

text: Okay. 24 10. Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. P52 and optics calibration attitude: roll 330.5, pitch 086.3, yaw 000.0. The nominal attitude that's pen-and-inked in for the P23 is still good. At time 25 30, approximately, after you complete P23, we're requesting a waste-water dump down to a nominal 25 percent. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Did you copy the attitudes and the waste-water dump? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger, Bruce. ...

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. Standing by.

speaker: CC

speaker: CMP

speaker: CC

speaker: CMP

speaker: CC

speaker: CC

speaker: CMP

speaker: CC
text: Okay. From Jodrell Bank, England, via AP: Britain's big Jodrell Bank radio telescope stopped receiving signals from the Soviet Union's unmanned Moon shot at 5:49 EDT today. A spokesman said that it appeared the Luna 15 space ship "had gone beyond the Moon." Another Quote: "We don't think it has landed," said a spokesman for Sir Bernard Lovell, Director of the Observatory. Washington UPI: Vice President Spiro T. Agnew has called for putting a man on Mars by the year 2000, but Democratic leaders replied that priority must go to needs on Earth. Agnew, ranking government official at the Apollo 11 blastoff Wednesday, apparently was speaking for himself and not necessarily for the Nixon administration when he said, "We should, in my judgment, put a man on Mars by the end of this century." Laredo, Texas, AP: Immigration officials in Nuevo Laredo announced Wednesday that hippies will be refused tourist cards to enter Mexico unless they take a bath and get haircuts. Huberto Cazaras, Chief of Mexican Immigration in Nuevo Laredo, said authorities in Mexico City, Acapulco, and other popular tourist spots have registered complaints about the hippies. By United Press International: Initial reaction to President Nixon's granting of a holiday Monday to Federal employees so they can observe a national day of participation in the Apollo 11 Moon landing mission mostly was one of surprise. Rodney Bidner, Associated Press, London AP: Europe is Moon struck by the Apollo 11 mission. Newspapers throughout the continent fill their pages with pictures of the Saturn V rocket blasting off to forge Earth's first link with its natural satellite. And the headline writers taxed their imagination for words to hail the feat. "The greatest adventure in the history of humanity has started," declared the French newspaper Le Figaro, which devoted four pages to reports from Cape Kennedy and diagrams of the mission. The tabloid Paris Jour proclaimed, "The whole word tells them bravo." The Communists daily L'Humanite led with the launch picture and devoted its entire back page to an enthusiastic Moon report describing the countdown and launch, the astronauts' wives and families, and backgrounding lunar activities.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. Thank you, Bruce. Another thing on that number 2 item, we all ... before we left, and we hope we get a chance to see him another time. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. And I understand he was down there and really enjoyed watching the launch. We all think it was pretty magnificent, and you all are doing great job up there.

speaker: CDR

text: Roger. Mike, we've got some comments on performance of P23 for today if you've got a minute to talk.

speaker: CDR
text: He's all ears.

speaker: CMP
text: Yes. Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. For today, we'd like you on P23 to make a trunnion bias determination, prior to P23 sightings as called out in procedures, and also one afterwards. Our intent here is to check out the possibility that some sort of thermal effect may be giving you errors in the angular read-out in the sextant. The bias that you get beforehand should be incorporated, that is a PROCEED on NOUN 87 after you get two consecutive measurements equal to within 0.003 degrees. And, of course, move the trunnion off a couple of degrees between the measurements. The Earth should be a lot smaller in your field of view today. I'm , sure you're a lot more qualified to tell us about that than we are, but to ensure that you're getting a good angle measurement between the star and the Earth horizon, the sextant M-line, which is the line that runs through the two hash marks and is perpendicular to the R-line, should be parallel to the Earth horizon at the substellar point. And then the actual superimposition of the star upon the horizon can be made at any point in the field of view of the sextant: above, below, or on the M-line. We recommend the marks be made as rapidly as possible after AUTO maneuver. If you feel that the amount of time between the AUTO maneuver and the time you get ready to mark is excessive, or that you don't like that AUTO maneuver attitude when you get ready to mark, of course, you can use a VERB 94 - VERB 94 to get you back to the flashing 51 position to redo the AUTO maneuvers. Over.

speaker: CMP

speaker: CC
text: Okay.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11.

speaker: CC

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. We're stopping PTC now and maneuvering to our P52 and optics CAL attitude. In regard to that P23, what I was trying to tell you yesterday was about that. The M-line is not anywhere parallel to the horizon at the roll, pitch, and yaw which you gave me to go to for the substellar point, and I was trying to maneuver off to get it parallel to the horizon when you all said that was not necessary.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. I guess in keeping the cups of coffee score, why you get that one.

speaker: CMP
text: Well - Okay - Well, this morning, let's just see how close it comes to being parallel to the M-line. Before we started marking for the first time, it appeared that the computation of - of those three angles was somewhat off, and that I was wasting a lot of gas by going to those three angles and then having to make large attitude changes after that to get the M-line parallel. In some cases it appeared to be just an accepted attitude required, and you all said that it wasn't needed. So I was marking in some cases with the M-line not parallel. I thought perhaps you had some processor for computing that offset and making sense out of that data, but as far as I know, we've got to have the M-line parallel to the horizon.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. We don't have that capability. We do require that the M-line be parallel to the horizon in order to get a good mark. We feel that possibly the - the state vector information that you were using for your maneuver basis yesterday may have needed to be updated a little. And if you'll standby a second, we'll give you an evaluation of what we feel you'll get today by the AUTO maneuver.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CMP

speaker: CMP

speaker: CC
text: When you move into P23, we recommend that you use the CMC-computed angles for your AUTO maneuver and see how that works out. If it doesn't bring you up with the M-line parallel to the horizon to the substellar point, we will see if we can get you some ground-computed angles. I guess the big thing here is to make sure that the M-line is parallel to substellar points so we can get a good angular measurement. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Yes. I believe.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Over.

speaker: CMP

speaker: CC

speaker: CC

speaker: CMP

speaker: CC
text: You are not getting any reflections or anything like that that would obscure your vision, are you?

speaker: CMP
text: Well, of course, the Earth is pretty bright, and the black sky, instead of being black, has sort of a rosy glow to it. The star, unless it is a very bright one, is probably lost somewhere in that glow, but it is just not visible. I maneuvered the reticle considerably above the horizon to make sure that the star is not lost in the brightness below the horizon. However, even when I get the reticle considerably above the horizon so the star should be seen against the black background, it still is not visible.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy. Standby a minute, please.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. Can you read us the shaft and trunnion angle off the counters?

speaker: CMP
text: Yes. I will be glad to. Shaft 331.2 and trunnion 35.85.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Thank you.

text: It's really a fantastic sight through that sextant. A minute ago, during that AUTO maneuver, the reticle swept across the Mediterranean. You could see all of North Africa, absolutely clear; all of Portugal, Spain, southern France; all of Italy, absolutely clear. Just a beautiful sight.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We all envy you the view up there.

speaker: CMP
text: But still no star.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. Go ahead, Bruce.

speaker: CC
text: On our ground computers we confirm the shaft and trunnion angle that you have as being pointed at the star. speaker: CMP

speaker: CC

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP

speaker: CC

speaker: CDR

speaker: CC

speaker: CMP

speaker: CC
text: Okay. Roger. Out.

text: Houston, Apollo 11. How do you read high gain?

speaker: CC
text: Read you loud and clear on high gain down here, and everything's looking good from our standpoint for your burn. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay, Bruce.

speaker: CDR
text: Houston, burn completed. You copying our residuals?

speaker: CC
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: CDR
text: And, Houston, looked like we saw about 87 or 88 psi on chamber pressure that time. I'd like you to look at that on the ground.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. We'll take a look at that and get back in a few minutes.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. On our real-time telemetry we saw 95 to 97 psi on chamber pressure. We'll - We will look at the recordings down here, thought, and get back with you again. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: And we've copied your residuals, 11.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. No, we're not going to trim those ...

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Could we get your DELTA-V counter reading, please, from this burn?

speaker: LMP
text: That's minus 3.8.

speaker: CC
text: Minus 2.8?

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Copy minus 3.8.

speaker: CDR
text: Houston, is there anything else you need on the burn status report?

speaker: CC
text: This is Houston. Negative, 11.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. Apollo 11.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. I just wanted to remind you that we haven't noticed on the TM the VERB 66 after the burn. And for your information, we played the recorded TV back last night, I believe, after you all turned in for your rest period, and the pictures came out quite well. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Did you get any usable pictures out of MILA on that first pass?

speaker: CC
text: Not that we've seen. We had word on the voice loop that MILA reported that they had gotten a minute's worth of TV signal, and Goldstone reported that they had gotten about a minute's worth of modulation but that they weren't able to get anything off of it.

speaker: CMP
text: 0kay. Thanks.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. We have another input here, 11, that the MILA data was recognizable as a picture, but we don't have any evaluation as to the quality of the picture. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: And for our information, we've been watching a PCO2 again. Did you change a lithium hydroxide canister this morning? Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Yes. We did, and we've been seeing 1.7 percent in the spacecraft ever since.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. That agrees with our data.

speaker: CDR
text: 1.7 millimeters.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy.

speaker: CDR
text: Houston, Apollo 11. We're starting our maneuver to PTC attitude.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. From a propellant-balancing standpoint, we recommend that you use quads Alfa and Bravo to start the PTC maneuvers. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Understand Alfa and Bravo.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Out.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. For CRYO-balancing purposes, we'd like you to turn the heater and oxygen tank number 1 off at this time. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: Everything else in the CRYO system remains the same.

speaker: CDR
text: 0kay.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. We have O2 heater tank 1 off.

speaker: CC
text: Houston. Roger. Out.

speaker: CMP
text: How is EECOMM today? Is he happy with all those good things?

speaker: CC
text: Oh, EECOMM is happy, and after you get PTC set up, we've got a little procedure from EEC0MM here to check out the O2 flow and the O2 flow sensor in your cabin enrichment. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CMP
text: It'll be a while, Bruce. We're just now arriving in PTC attitude, and we're going to our 20 minutes of monitoring thruster activity.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy. He'll be here.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. Are you going to take control of the 0MNI's now and switch us between B and D?

speaker: CC
text: This is Houston. Stand by one.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston.

speaker: CMP
text: Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Mike, how about selecting Bravo at this time, and I'll give you a COMP configuration here, shortly.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CMP
text: That PTC sure worked well last night.

speaker: CC
text: Outstanding.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston.

speaker: CMP
text: Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. Roll for the COMM situation: have S-band antenna OMNI A in Bravo, S-band antenna OMNI to OMNI, high-gain track to MANUAL, and the pitch is minus 50 and yaw is 270.

speaker: CMP
text: You may have to repeat some of that, James. We've got a LM guy taking care of the high gain right now.

speaker: CDR
text: Yes, and he is eyeballing the Earth.

speaker: CMP
text: He's got his head out the window.

speaker: CC
text: I understand, I had trouble on 12 with him, too.

speaker: LMP
text: Say again what you'd like.

speaker: CC
text: Okay, The S-band antenna OMNI A switch to Bravo which you have now, and S-band antenna OMNI to the 0MNI position, and the high-gain track to the MANUAL position, and the pitch and yaw angles are minus 50 for pitch and yaw is 270.

speaker: LMP
text: Minus 50 and 270.

speaker: LMP
text: Hey, Jim, I'm looking through the monocular now, and to coin an expression, the view is just beautiful. It's out of this world. I can see all the islands in the Mediterranean. Some larger and smaller islands of Majorca, Sardinia, and Corsica.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. I understand that the Northern Africa - Mediterranean area is fairly clear today, huh?

speaker: LMP
text: Right.

speaker: CDR
text: Yes. We see a bunch of roads with cars driving up and down, too.

speaker: CC
text: Do you find that the monocular is any good to you, Buzz?

speaker: LMP
text: Yes, It would be nicer if it had another order of magnitude of power on it. Of course, it has a tendency to jiggle around a little bit, and you might want to have some sort of a bracket. I hate to use that word though.

speaker: LMP
text: Got an anticyclone going in the southern hemisphere southeast of Brazil, and some - Well, the diameter of it must be over 2000 miles across.

speaker: CC
text: How does the weather look up in the southern part of the western hemisphere, or up in the United States area?

speaker: LMP
text: Well, you all are just beginning to come over the limb now. I can see parts of Central America, and it looks to be fairly clear there. The islands in the Caribbean are beginning to come in and rather a few streaming lines of clouds. Looks like there is a system up to the - well, off of Greenland that has some large cloud streamers extending back down to the southwest. The east coast of the U.S. is just coming into view now, and it doesn't look too bad that I can see right now. We may have some pretty good shots later on this afternoon. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Thank you.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11.

speaker: CC
text: Go ahead, 11.

speaker: LMP
text: I've got a comment about the point on the Earth where the Sun's rays reflect back up toward us. In general, the color of the oceans is mostly uniform and it's bright and darker blue except for that region that's about one-eighth of an Earth's radius in diameter; and in this circular area, the blue of the water turns a grayish color, and I'm sure that's where the Sun's rays are being reflected back on up toward us. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Buzz. We noticed the same thing. It's very similar to looking at a light shining on something like a billiard ball or a bowling ball. You get this bright spot in the blue of the water, and that turns it to sort of a grayish color.

speaker: LMP
text: Yes. Is there a Navy term for that?

speaker: CC
text: (Laughing.) A lot of gray paint.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston.

speaker: CMP
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: CC
text: Mike, are you satisfied with P23 now?

speaker: CMP
text: Yes, I'm happy with the last updates we got, you know, in terms of what it did to our state vector. Still not altogether happy with the various procedures. If we could pick stars within the smaller range of trunnion angles so that you could allow P23 to pick its own maneuver and go to that substellar point and then have that star visible, that would seem to me to be the simplest and best way to do it.

speaker: CC
text: How about the - -

speaker: LMP
text: ... correction on that last ...

speaker: CC
text: How about the horizon now? Is it pretty well defined for you and no longer hazy?

speaker: CMP
text: Yes. We're far enough out now that the - I think the horizon definition variation is lost in the North.

speaker: LMP
text: Hey, Jim.

speaker: CC
text: Go ahead, Buzz.

speaker: LMP
text: Looks like the best way to get a steady view through the monocular is just steady it out and let it close when it's in front of your eye, and then you kind of float up next to it so that you're not touching it at all. It has a very slow drift, and you get a better - steadier view that way.

speaker: CC
text: Sounds good.

speaker: CC
text: How does it feel to be airborne again, Buzz?

speaker: LMP
text: Well, I'll tell you, I've been having a ball floating around inside here, back and forth up to one place and back to another. It's like being outside, except more comfortable.

speaker: CC
text: It's a lot bigger than our last vehicle.

speaker: CMP
text: ... kept me busy, I'm ...

speaker: CMP
text: Say again about Buzz -

speaker: LMP
text: Yes. It sure is nice in here.

speaker: CC
text: I said it's a lot bigger than the last vehicle that Buzz and I were in.

speaker: CMP
text: Oh, yes. It's been nice. I've been very busy so far. I'm looking forward to taking the afternoon off. I've been cooking, and sweeping, and almost sewing, and you know, the usual little housekeeping things.

speaker: CC
text: It was very convenient the way they put the food preparation system right next to the NAV station.

speaker: CDR
text: Everything is right next to everything in this vehicle.

speaker: LMP
text: Not if you're in the ...

speaker: CDR
text: Jim, it's been a little warm in the machine throughout yesterday and last night during the PTC. It cooled off somewhat with the windows buttoned up, and we've seen suit temperatures of about - the high 40's and cabin temperatures in the low 60's. But this seems to be still a little bit on the warm side.

speaker: CC
text: I understand that it got a little warm during the day and cooled down a little bit when you put the shades up, but you're still a little bit warm. Do you have any moisture condensation or anything like that on the wall?

speaker: CDR
text: No, we haven't been able to detect any moisture anyplace in the spacecraft. It seems to be fine.

speaker: LMP
text: One of the hydrogen filters - the one that we've got on the hot water - seems to keep flowing when you remove one of the food bags from it. Its flow rate is quite small, right near the end of one out, and that contributes a little bit of moisture to the atmosphere.

speaker: CMP
text: Yes, that hydrogen thing, it's - I'm not sure, but I think it's a backpressure problem. If the thing sees any backpressure at all, like when the bag is attached, well the flow rate will slowly decrease to where it's almost zero, and you wait, and you wait, and you wait for that last ounce. You think you have its and you remove the bag, and then you very rapidly thereafter see maybe a glob the size of a dime or a quarter come out and just hang there. That appears to be true even though the opening into the bag is not restricted.

speaker: CC
text: Understand.

speaker: LMP
text: In general, I think they do quite a good job, especially on the guns, in removing a lot of the hydrogen bubbles.

speaker: CC
text: Have the water temperatures been good? Are you getting hot water?

speaker: LMP
text: Yes. It seems reasonably warm.

speaker: CMP
text: We made three cups of coffee today. The last one - you know when all the plumbing was warmed up, the hydrogen gun and everything, was warmest of the three. I don't know who had that one - Neil, did you have that one? How was your coffee? You didn't drink it till later, did you? Anyway, it's pretty good. It's not piping hot, but it sure beats stone-cold coffee.

speaker: CMP
text: Jim, we've been sitting here a little over 20 minutes now, How does the thruster firing activity look? Are you ready to go on with this PTC?

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: We're all set to go, Mike.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. I'll press on then.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. PTC has started and it looks good.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Roger. This is Houston. Roger. Out.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. If you're free for a couple of minutes, we have a procedure here that will let us verify the O2 flow transducer and at the same time get some more of our cabin enrichment out of the way. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Stand by.

speaker: CDR
text: Go ahead, Houston. We're ready to copy.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. The primary purpose of this is, as I mentioned, to let us check out your O2 flow transducer. However, we still need about 2 hours' worth of cabin enrichment, so we'd like to keep the vent that we're going to set up going for this purpose. Okay. We want you to install the cabin vent quick disconnect which you'll find in compartment R-6, that is Romeo 6, on the urine connector on panel 251. When this is completed, verify that the waste stowage vent valve is closed, and then open or position the waste management overboard drain to the DUMP position. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. Understand that. Install the cabin quick disconnect out of R-6 on the 251 urine connector and verify that the waste dump valve is closed, and say again the last part.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. And then put the waste management overboard drain valve into the DUMP position. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. Put the waste management overboard drain valve to the DUMP position.

speaker: CC
text: Right. That's the one down on panel 251 also. And we'll watch your O2 flow on telemetry down here.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay, Houston. That configuration is set up.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. Say again, please.

speaker: CDR
text: You do have the O2 flow transducer checkout setup accomplished.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. Understand you have opened the drain valve at this time.

speaker: CDR
text: That's ... It's in DUMP.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We're not getting telemetry data from you right due to low signal strength. There it comes back. I expect it'll probably take us anywhere from 15 minutes to half an hour to see an increase in O2 flow due to the size of the cabin and of course of the small size of the drain. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11.

speaker: CC
text: Go ahead, 11.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. I've got the world in my window for a change and looking at it through the monocular, it's really something. I wish I could describe it properly. The weather is very good. South America is coming around into view. I can see on the - what appears to me to be upper horizon, a point that must be just about Seattle, Washington, and from there I can see all the way down to the southern tip of Tierra del Fuego and the southern tip of the continent.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Sounds like you've got a beautiful view up there.

speaker: CMP
text: Absolutely fantastic. I hope the pictures come out. We,re rotating around where it's going out of view again.

speaker: LMP
text: I'm waiting to pick it up in the sextant.

speaker: CC
text: Sounds like one of these rotating restaurants.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. Do you need some help keeping OMNI's locked on us?

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Negative. We had a command computer at the Madrid site go down. We had to switch over to Ascension temporarily. We're now back remoting through Madrid, and the computer is back, and we're ready to resume control of your OMNI's and full communication. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. You've got it.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. One thing that we did miss in the dropout in the noise here is your LM/CM DELTA-P reading for about 28 hours GET. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. The LM/CM DELTA-P is 0.98.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. 0.98, and what have you been reading for O2 flow on your onboard gage? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Well, right now, after we put that gadget in, we've got it back to 0.35. Before that, we were reading on scale level. I think ours is relatively correct, at least when time comes for the water accumulator to kick in at 10 seconds, it goes on up to about 0.75, 0.8, something like that.

speaker: CC
text: This is Houston. Roger. Out.

speaker: CC
text: And, 11, this is Houston. A little more information based on our analysis of your last SPS burn: it looks like you got a good solid burn there. We show 94 psi chamber pressure and it looks like the SPS is definitely GO. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Good to heer it.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We thought you'd feel that way about it.

speaker: LMP
text: We're right in the middle of - well either ... or salmon salad, or something like that. That's probably why we're not answering you right away.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. Well, we don't want - -

speaker: LMP
text: My compliments to the chef, that salad salmon is outstanding.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Understand that's the salad salmon. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Something like that, salmon salad.

speaker: CC
text: There we go, the salmon salad, very good.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. Bruce, we're coming up on the water accumulator activity, and it's going on up to 0.85, oh, about 0.95 and it reached a peak there and then gradually dropped back on down to 0.6 now, 0.4, and it looks like it's pretty well - pretty well leveling off back down to 0.35. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, We're copying that.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston.

speaker: CDR
text: Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. On that 2O flow transducer down here on telemetry, our values are agreeing pretty well with what you read out onboard, and the EECOMM's have been noticing this cycle, but it still looks like the indicated rate is lower than what we would expect. We're still working on the problem, and we'll let you have a more complete diagnosis on it in a little while.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. It's a tight fix then.

speaker: CMP
text: We run a tight ship.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Is that music I hear in the background?

speaker: CMP
text: Buzz in singing.

speaker: CC
text: Okay.

speaker: CMP
text: Pass me the sausage, man.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. We've been watching your activity on the DSKY there, and by selecting another major program with a VERB 37 ENTER and all that, we show you collapsing the deadband in PTC and having driven the CMC rate from 0.3 degrees per second down to 0 degrees per second, although of course, with all the AUTO RCS coils shut off, you're not firing any thrusters. 0ver.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. What do you recommend?

speaker: CC
text: Well, you can just continue in your present configuration in PTC. However, if you go to turn any thrusters on, the CMC would then try to bring you into an attitude hold position rather than continuing with the PTC. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. I understand.

speaker: CC
text: Okay.

speaker: CDR
text: And, Houston, we're just looking at you out our window here. Looks like there's a circulation of clouds that just moved east of Houston over the Gulf and Florida area. Did that have any rain in it this morning?

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Our report from outside says that it's raining out here, and looks like you've got a pretty good eye for the weather there.

speaker: CDR
text: Yes. Well, it looks like it ought to clear up pretty soon from our viewpoint. The western edge of the weather isn't wery far west of you.

speaker: CC
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. As a result of our venting through the waste management drain, we've concluded that your O2 flow rate sensor is, in fact, malfunctioning. I mentioned when you talked us through the cyclic water accumulator dump that even though it was moving, probably indicating a higher flow rate, it didn't seem to be indicating a flow rate that is high enough; and based on that and the flow that we're getting right now, we've concluded that the transducer is malfunctioning. We'd like to continue the O2 flow for about another hour, shutting it off at about 31 hours GET, to get the O2 concentration in the vehicles up to - in the vehicles up to where it will be acceptable for LM checkout. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. Does it look to you like it just has a bias on it?

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. It does seem to be a bias. Looks like it has a fairly high threshold before it starts indicating. EECOMM seems to think, though, that for high flow rate purposes, it will still give you a relative indication during the mission. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. We understand. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We would like you to terminate charging on battery A at GET 30 plus 15. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. 30 plus 15 for battery A charge terminate.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Out.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. If you're free for a minute, I've got some updates to the P37 PAD's that we passed up to you yesterday afternoon, I guess. As a result of doing midcourse correction number 2, the DELTA-V required in the TLI plus 35, 44, and 53 PAD's have changed slightly. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. Standing by to copy.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. TLI plus 35 PAD: the DELTA-VT should be 7992 instead of 8016. TLI plus 44 - It should be 6112 instead of 6141. And TLI plus 53 - It should be 8172 instead of 8209. Read back. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. Understand. 7992, 6112, 8172. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Readback correct. Out.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. Goldstone reports they are receiving a TV picture coming down from you all, a little snowy, but a good TV picture. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. We're just testing the equipment up here.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CDR
text: Ask them if they can read the numbers.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: Goldstone, this is Houston CAP C0MM. Over.

speaker: CT
text: Houston CAP COMM, Goldstone M&O. Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Stand by a minute, Goldstone.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. What numbers are you referring to? Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Well, I guess if they can't see any numbers, why, it's kind of a lost cause.

speaker: CC
text: Negative. Standby. We wanted to know - -

speaker: CC
text: We wanted to know what numbers before we asked them.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. I'm showing them the DSKY, and I'd like to know whether they can read what's showing on the DSKY, and also whether they can see P-R-O-G, V-E-R-B, and N-O-U-N. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Stand by a second.

speaker: CC
text: Goldstone M&O, Houston CAP COMM. Over.

speaker: CT
text: CAP COMM, Goldstone. Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Did you copy the spacecraft request?

speaker: CT
text: That's affirmative. I am reading the numbers on our monitor here.

speaker: CC
text: Okay, that's - Roger. That's both the numbers on the DSKY itself, and the little words like PROGRAM and VERB, NOUN, COMPUTER ACTIVITY, things of this sort?

speaker: CT
text: Roger. I can read the numbers clearly. We can't distinguish what the words are, because it is a little snowy.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CT
text: Okay. I read VERB, NOUN, and PROGRAM.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Do you see - Over in the lefthand corner, there's a big square one that says COMPUTER ACTIVITY, COMP ACTIVITY?

speaker: CT
text: Roger. I see a flash occasionally in that area.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. that's the one.

speaker: CT
text: Okay. It looks like he's moved the camera at this time.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. Goldstone M&0 reports that they can read the numbers on the DSKY. They can also read VERB, NOUN, PROGRAM, and see the COMP ACTIVITY light flashing. 0vet.

speaker: CDR
text: Very good. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: And they also report you appear to have panned the camera over to another location now.

speaker: CDR
text: Yes, we're going to work on something else.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11.

speaker: CC
text: Go ahead, 11.

speaker: CMP
text: Oh, Charlie. That you?

speaker: CC
text: That's me. How are you there?

speaker: CMP
text: Oh, Just fine. How's the old White Team today?

speaker: CC
text: Oh, the old White Team's bright-eyed and bushytailed. We're ever alert down here.

speaker: CMP
text: Ever alert and ... Hey, you got any medics down there watching high grade? I'm trying to do some running in place down here, and I'm wondering just out of curiosity whether it brings my heart rate up.

speaker: CC
text: Well, they will spring into action here momentarily. Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, 11. We see your heart beating.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay, Well - look at the CDR 's and the CMP 's and see if they go up any. We're all running in place up here. You wouldn't believe it.

speaker: CC
text: I'd like to see that sight. Why don't you give us a TV picture of that one.

speaker: CMP
text: I think Buzz is trying. You got it.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. It's coming in at Goldstone, Buzz. As Bruce, said, we don't have it here in the center.

speaker: CMP
text: I'm afraid this isn't going to help out the PTC very much.

speaker: CMP
text: Yes. I don't know if it's a vibration or what it is, but it makes the pitch and yaw rate needles on FDAI number 1 jump up and down a little bit where we jump up and down.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Goldstoners say they see you running there, Mike.

speaker: CMP
text: 0kay.

speaker: CDR
text: Ask him what he's running from.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Mike, we see about a 96 heartbeat now.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Thank you.

speaker: CMP
text: Well, that's about all that is reasonable, without getting hot and sweaty.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy.

speaker: CMP
text: Goldstone should be getting about the best picture of the Earth we can give them right now, Charlie.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Mike. Thank you much.

speaker: LMP
text: We've got a tittle distortion in the horizontal direction from banding on our monitor. I wonder if they're getting the same thing?

speaker: CC
text: Stand by, Buzz. I'll let you know.

speaker: LMP
text: I guess it would be more described as a waviness.

speaker: CC
text: Goldstone M&O, Houston CAP COMM.

speaker: CT
text: Goldstone M&O.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. The crew is complaining of some horizontal banding on their monitor. Do you see that on the picture?

speaker: CT
text: Stand by.

speaker: LMP
text: They wouldn't see anything now. We don't have anything in focus, Charlie.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. He's checking on it. I'll see if they had it earlier. Stand by.

speaker: CMP
text: I guess when we're showing the DSKY or when we're showing the Earth might be the better time.

speaker: CC
text: Okay.

speaker: CT
text: Houston CAP COMM, Goldstone.

speaker: CC
text: Go ahead.

speaker: CT
text: Okay. Our TV people confirm they see this horizontal band.

speaker: CC
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. The Goldstone TV people also see the banding when - at the same time you do. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. Would they call it a horizontal waviness, instead of banding, maybe?

speaker: CC
text: I'm not talking to them directly. Stand by, Buzz. Let me see how they describe it.

speaker: CC
text: Goldstone M&0, Houston CAP COMM. Could you put the TV guy on the loop, please?

speaker: CT
text: CAP C0MM, Goldstone. Roger.

speaker: CT
text: Houston CAP COMM, Goldstone M&0 NET 1.

speaker: CC
text: Go.

speaker: CT
text: The TV people do not have access to NET 1 in that area. Suggest we use NET 2 For that purpose.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. Going to NET 2.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. The Goldstone TV guys say they have some horizontal banding across the upper part of the picture and across the lower part. They would consider the lines just straight, no waviness to them at all. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Understand. They do seem to distort vertical lines though.

speaker: CC
text: Say again about the vertical lines, Buzz.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. When there's a vertical line, these horizontal bands tend to put small waves in it.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. I copy. He didn't mention that. Stand by, I'll check again.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, 11. Houston. The Goldstone TV said that when you get a sharp vertical line on the picture, when the horizontal banding goes across, it does appear to bend it slightly. The same as Apollo 10, they said. Looks okay to them. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. Understand. It's not our monitor. It must be the transmitter or the system.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. I guess so, Buzz. We'll have them look into it, and see if they can suggest anything.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We've lost our command interface with Goldstone. We'd like you to switch to 0MNI Delta. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Going to Delta.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We'd like you to terminate the O2 purge if you have not done so already, and the TV camera people say that the lines are inherent in the camera, Buzz; and it's something that we expected. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Understand about the camera. Say again about the O2 purge.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We can terminate the O2 purge at this time. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Oh, okay. Fine. Will do.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Please select OMNI Bravo on board. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Going to Bravo, Charlie.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: How's everything going down there? You guys happy with the spacecraft systems?

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Affirmative. Everything's looking really good to us. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Same here.

speaker: CMP
text: Charlie, how far out can you pick up TV off the 0MNI?

speaker: CC
text: Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We're just about to the limits where we can get any kind of picture at all on the OMNI's on the TV. It - The picture, I guess, would be just almost zero at this point.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Well, for this TV program coming up in a couple of hours, you might give some thought to how you want us to stop PTC, if you do, for the best high gain angle; and also it would be nice if you could stop us at such an attitude that we'd have the Earth out of one of our windows.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. We're thinking about that.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We got some PIPA biases and general drift updates for you if you give us P00 and ACCEPT. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay, Charlie. Stant by one.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. The - -

speaker: CDR
text: You've got it.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. Thank you much. Our biggest drift on the GYRO's is 0.03 degrees per hour with - on the X-GYRO. On the PIPA's, the Y-PIPA's the biggest and it's 0.006 feet per second so ... trying to tweak it up. The biggest we have is about one sigma on both GYRO's and accelerometers.

speaker: CDR
text: Sounds good.

speaker: CC
text: The system really looks good to us.

speaker: CDR
text: Glad to hear it, Charlie.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. You can go back to BLOCK. We've got the load in.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: Boy, you sure get a different perspective in this thing in zero g. Right now, Neil's got his feet on the forward hatch, and he can with his arms reach - all five windows, He can reach down into - the LEB where the overboard drain is. He can practically reach over in the cockpit.

speaker: CC
text: Sounds like Plastic Man to me.

speaker: CMP
text: I'm hiding under the left-hand couch trying to stay out of his way.

speaker: CC
text: Be a good idea, Mike.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. You got a cloud over the Houston area right now?

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We just had a really big thunderstorm here about a hour ago. Couple of storms around the area ... Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Yes. I see one fairly large and isolated one. There are couple of more off to the left, but this one looks fairly good size. It could very well be the one that just passed over you.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: Yes, and it looks like the Cape has been having a little bit of rain, too.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. The one we had here came in from the west and is moving east - or nearly so, as far as I could tell.

speaker: LMP
text: That view through this sextant is fantastic. I can see Alaska right up - right up along the LM, and I'm running the crosshairs right now down the coast of California, the west coast of Mexico, Yucatan Peninsula, up around the Gulf, Florida, Cuba, down Central America, and I'm running into the stop right now, on the sextant.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. It sounds like a pretty fantastic view.

speaker: LMP
text: The guys in the weather office at Patrick wanted a report on the tops but I guess all we can say is we're above them.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We'll pass it on to METRO.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Do you see any predominant weather systems as far as frontal type or any buildup of tropical-storm type? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Not any large ones. There are a couple of smaller disturbances. Well, there's one maybe 300 miles north of Cuba, but it doesn't look cyclonic.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We got a TV attitude for you and also an update to your CMC erasable load and your alternate contingency checklist, if you could break that out too. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. I'm not sure I caught all of that. Go ahead with what you have.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. If you'll break out your alternate and contingency checklist for the CSM, we got an update to some of the erasable loads on page F2-20, Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. Be getting that out, and you can give us the attitude for TV.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. Your TV attitude will be roll 261, pitch 090, yaw 000. High gain angle: pitch plus 28, yaw 271. That puts the left-hand window pointed at the Earth. We recommend exiting PTC with your updated procedure in the checklist. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. We copy roll 21 - 61, pitch 090, yaw 000, high gain pitch plus 28, yaw 271. And we'll like this with the DELTA-V that we have in the book. Over.

speaker: CC
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: CMP
text: Charlie, Apollo 11. I have a couple of questions on stopping the PTC. It seems to me the easiest way to stop it would be - we're essentially, of course, at 0 degrees yaw and closing up to 90 degrees pitch, so it's just a question of stopping at 260 roll, roughly, and - How about for a procedure going MANUAL ATTITUDE, three to RATE COMMAND and then, seeing as how our deadband has already collapsed, I'll turn on the panel 8 RCS thrusters, at which time it should stop at whatever attitude it finds itself in. And if I do all of that as it comes up on 261 degrees roll, we should stop right there. Is that sufficient?

speaker: CC
text: Sounds pretty good. Stand by one.

speaker: CMP
text: Sounds like it might save a little gas.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. What page do you want in that revision? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. If you'll turn to page F2-20. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay, Tim -

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. Under column A on page F2-20, line 5, line 05, the new data is 01042; line 07, the new data is 00256. Skipping down to line 11, 00070; line 12 is 00042; line 13 is 77730. In column Bravo, lines 3, 4, and 5, which are blank, should be all zeros for line 3; line 4 is 20017; line 5 20616. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Good readback, Buzz. And stand by, Mike, on the coming-out-of-the-PTC recommendation. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Fine.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston with a recommendation on exiting PTCM. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Mike. We'd like to see you go to ACCEL COMMAND on the MANUAL ATTITUDE switches. Then to turn on the AUTO RCS SELECT switches, and then go RATE COMMAND. That will prevent us from firing jets uncoupled. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Fine. And I would guess go RATE COMMAND and roll first and then followed by pitch and yaw.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. That sounds good if - And when you get to the roll attitude desired, just go RATE COMMAND at that time and it'll stop us right on.

speaker: CMP
text: Yes. I agree, Charlie. That sounds right.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston with some more words on exiting PTC. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Go ahead, Charlie.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Mike, when you were playing with the P37 a while ago and we collapsed the deadband back down, the DAP assumed that the deadband was centered around the new attitude that we happened to be at, at that time. Since then, we've drifted out a couple of degrees in both pitch and yaw from that attitude such that if we did the procedure as we called it up to you of going ACCEL COMMAND, turning on all of the AUTO RCS SELECT switches and then RATE COMMAND, it would attempt to fly back to the pitch and yaw attitude that it had when the deadband collapsed. We can prevent that by - just immediately prior to going to RATE COMMAND on the MANUAL ATTITUDE switches, if you cycle the SPACECRAFT CONTROL switch to SCS, then back to CMC. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Sounds like a winner.

speaker: CC
text: Okay.

speaker: CMP
text: I'm not going to let these LM guys play with my DSKY anymore.

speaker: CC
text: You sound like you'd better protect it. It looks like just about anything that you do with that DSKY is going to collapse that deadband back down.

speaker: CMP
text: Understand.

speaker: CMP
text: Charlie, we just STABED to 261 degrees roll, and it looks like whoever figured it out did a good Job. It's right there, dab-smack in the middle of window number 1.

speaker: CC
text: Sounds great.

speaker: LMP
text: Looks like Houston's still got a little smog over it, Charlie.

speaker: CC
text: We've got a constant overcast here in the room. We'll be right there. Stand by.

speaker: LMP
text: Of course, a little cloud from up here probably covers 8 or 10 states.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Some of our guys just came in from outside and said it's pretty clear over the center here. It's cleared up completely. All the storms have moved on.

speaker: LMP
text: Very good.

speaker: LMP
text: Oh, yes, Charlie. I can see it through the sextant now, and I can see the coastline is clear. Those clouds are just inland a few miles.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. We copy.

speaker: LMP
text: Looks like the southeast part of the country is all socked in.

speaker: LMP
text: California looks nice. The San Joaquin Valley shows up as a real dark spot with a lighter brown on either side of it. You can't tell that it's green. It looks just sort of dark gray or maybe even real dark blue.

speaker: CC
text: How does the Mojave look? Is it clear?

speaker: LMP
text: Yes. As usual.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. The - around -

speaker: LMP
text: It looks like there's some clouds just to the west of the Sierras, northeast of Bakersfield a little bit; and crossing over into the Mojave from Bakersfield looks clear; and then as you get on further to the southeast of there, there's a few clouds.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. Can you pick out Edwards in the sextant? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: I can see a 104 taxiing out for takeoff on the runway.

speaker: CC
text: Hey, man. That's super.

speaker: LMP
text: These dang bastards almost always have a 104 taxiing out for takeoff.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Could you pick out anything around Edwards, a dry lake or anything? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Negative, Charlie. I just - I don't have that resolution. But to give you some idea, I can - on the lower Texas coast, I can see - knowing what I'm looking for, I can see Padre Island. I can just barely make out the fact that there's a thin spit of land and then there's a little dark zone which is the Laguna Madre between it and the mainland.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. That's pretty significant. Thank you much, Buzz.

speaker: LMP
text: Right.

speaker: LMP
text: How far out are we, Charlie?

speaker: CC
text: Stand by. I'll give it to you exactly. Looks like around 130,000, but stand by.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. The exact range is 125,200 miles, and you're traveling 4486 feet per second.

speaker: LMP
text: Pretty far and pretty slow. Just past halfway.

speaker: LMP
text: Hey, Charlie, what the latest on Luna 15?

speaker: CC
text: Say again, Buzz? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. What's the latest on Luna 15?

speaker: CC
text: Stand by. I'll get the straight story for you.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Go ahead, Charlie.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Latest on Luna 15 - TASS reported this morning that the spacecraft was placed in orbit close to the lunar surface, and everything seems to be functioning normally on the vehicle. Sir Bernard Lovell said the craft appears to be in an orbit of about 62 nautical miles. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Thank you, Charlie.

speaker: CC
text: And also, President Nixon has reported - or declared a day of participation on Monday for all federal employees to enable everybody to follow your activities on the surface. Many state and city governments and businesses throughout the country are also giving their employees the day off, so it looks like you're going to have a pretty large audience for the EVA.

speaker: CMP
text: Oh, that's very nice, Charlie. I'll tell Neil about it.

speaker: CDR
text: Houston, Apollo 11. We've stopped PTC. We're in the right position; we're setting up for TV.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. We have you stopped in the PTC; attitude looks good to us. Mike, I would like to get a COMM check. The last couple of the transmissions from the spacecraft has been garbled from especially Buzz. Could you both give me a COMM check? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger, Charlie. Buzz here. How do you read? 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. You are about four-by with a slight decrease/increase in volume, sort of a wavy volume to it. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. I moved my mike around. How about now? Is this any better?

speaker: CC
text: Hey, that's beautiful right there. Thank you.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay, Charlie. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. How do you read me?

speaker: CC
text: Roger. You're five-by. Is Neil on?

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Neil. You're five-by.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We got the network all configured for the TV. You can start any time you want. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Okay, 11. We have a picture. We see the Earth right in the center of the screen. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger, Houston. Apollo 11 calling in from about 130,000 miles out. And we'll zoom our camera in slowly and get the most magnification we can. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. The definition is pretty good on our monitor here. The color is not too ..., at least on this set. Could you describe what you're looking at? Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. You're seeing Earth, as we see it, out our left-hand window, just a little more than a half Earth. We're looking at the eastern Pacific Ocean, and the north half of the top half of the screen, we can see North America, Alaska, United States, Canada, Mexico, and Central America. South America becomes invisible just off beyond the terminator or inside the shadow. We can see the oceans with a definite blue cast, see white bands of major cloud formations across the Earth, and can see coastlines, pick out the western U.S., San Joaquin Valley, the Sierra mountain range, the peninsula of Baja California, and we can see some cloud formations over southeastern U.S. There's one definite mild storm southwest of Alaska, looks like about 500 to 1000 miles, and another very minor storm showing the south end of the screen near the - or a long ways off of the equator, probably 45 degrees or more south latitude. Can pick out the browns in the landforms pretty well. Greens do not show up very well. Some greens showing along the northeastern - northwestern coast of the United States and northwestern coast of Canada.

speaker: CDR
text: Yes. They cross just south of the lower part of Mexico, probably through Central America. That is the equatorial band which we assume to be the intertropical convergence zone. The other band, which stands about 30 south, correctly appears to join the equator at the far left, or just beyond the horizon on the left edge of Earth, or at least it looks like it's going to join it. We don't have an explanation for that banding.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Neil. Thank you. It also appears that just to the left of the terminator, up in the northern hemisphere, there's a cloudband trending - a gap in the cloud, trending northwest/southeast. It appears to us that that comes in about over the northern United States, or perhaps the central United States. Is that about correct? Over.

speaker: CDR
text: I can see on the monitor the thing you were talking about, but right now I can't get my eye to the window to pick out just where it crosses the shoreline.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: You guys are doing a good job. It's a real steady picture, here. We're - Clarity is excellent. The color, it's - the clouds are - The whites are distinct. The rest if it looks like, to me anyway on the monitor I'm observing, is a fairly greenish blue is the way I'd describe it. Over.

speaker: CC
text: It appears that the - -

speaker: CDR
text: Well, we can't observe much green from the spacecraft.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. On this monitor, the landmasses appear to be just a darker grayish color rather than a brown.

speaker: CDR
text: Well, it's true that we do not have the depths of color at this range that we enjoyed at 50,000 miles out. However, the oceans still are a definite blue and the continents are generally brownish in cast,

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. We've been - I've just been vectored to another monitor and sure enough, the browns are coming in a lot more distinctly on the Eidephor that we have up on our screen in the control center. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay, world, hold on to your hat. I'm going to turn you upside-down.

speaker: CC
text: 11, that's a pretty good roll, there.

speaker: CDR
text: Oh, I'd say sloppy, Charlie. Let me try that one again.

speaker: CC
text: You'll never beat out the thunderbird.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. That practice did you some good. It's looking - real smooth roll, there.

speaker: CC
text: Oops! Spoke too soon.

speaker: CDR
text: I'm making myself seasick doing it, Charlie. I'll just put you back rightside-up where you belong.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CDR
text: You don't get to do that every day.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Could you describe, from your view, the polar cloudcap? It appears to us to extend down the western coast of North America. Would you estimate how far it extends down? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Trying to fit everybody into the window.

speaker: CDR
text: It appears that the cloudcap comes down a little bit below the southern extremity of Alaska.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: We've - 11, we've lost our picture here, now.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. Apollo 11, Houston. We've got the picture back now.

speaker: CDR
text: Unfortunately, we only have one window that has a view of the Earth and it's filled up with the TV camera, so your view now is probably better than ours is.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. If you could comply, we'd like to see a little smiling faces up there, if you could give us some interior views. I'm sure everybody would like to see you. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. We'll reconfigure the TV for that.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. It appears to us that we're seeing a view from outside plus a little of the inside. It appears you've taken the camera away from the left window now. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: That's correct. We're moving it back and reconfiguring for interior lighting.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: We can still see the Earth through the left window, and it appears that we can see a floodlight off to the left, either that or some Sun shafting through the hatch window.

speaker: CDR
text: It's a floodlight.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Now we're coming in. Can't quite make out who that ...

speaker: CC
text: That's big Mike Collins, there - -

speaker: CMP
text: You got a little bit of - Yes, hello there sports fans. You got a little bit of me, plus Neil is in the center couch, and Buzz is doing the camera work at this time.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. It's a little dark now, 11. Maybe a bigger f-stop might help.

speaker: CMP
text: Yes, that's in work.

speaker: CC
text: It's getting a lot better now, 11. Mike, you're coming in five-by. I got a good -

speaker: CMP
text: I would have put on a coat and tie if I'd known about this ahead of time.

speaker: CC
text: Is Buzz holding your cue cards for you. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Cue cards have a no. We have no intertions of competing with the professionals, believe me. We are very comfortable up here, though. We do have a happy home. There's plenty of room for the three of us and I think we're all learning to find our favorite little corner to sit in. Zero g is very comfortable, but after a while you get to the point where you sort of get tired of rattling around and banging off the ceiling and the floor and the side, so you tend to find a little corner somewhere and put your knees up or something like that to wedge yourself in, and that seems more at home.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Looks like Neil is coming in five-by there, 11. Mike, see you in the background. The definition is really outstanding. The colors are good. It's a real good picture we're getting here of Commander Armstrong. We - Buzz, when you take the camera over towards the window where the Sun's shafting through, it tends to blank it out, though.

speaker: CMP
text: Yes, Neil's standing on his head again. He's trying to make me nervous.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: He's disappearing up into the tunnel, of course, as he would going into the lunar module, only backwards.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We 'can see portions of the LEB now. The systems test meter panel, in the lower part of the picture, or we did have it, anyway.

speaker: CMP
text: 0kay. And directly behind his head are our optical instruments, the sextant and the telescope that we use to take sightings with.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Copy. And we see the DSKY flashing with a 651. In fact, we can read registers 1 and 2 quite clearly.

speaker: CMP
text: We have the old high gain angles telling us which way the Earth is.

speaker: CC
text: Copy. That's a beautiful picture. Clarity is outstanding.

speaker: CMP
text: We can also give you the time of day in our system of mission elapsed time. Elapsed time: 34 hours 16 minutes and umpteen seconds. Can you see that clearly enough, Charlie?

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Apollo 11. We can see it counting up every - every second. We got 34 17 02 now.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Back to the high-gain angles.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: Now we have amputated those.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We have a beautiful rainbow there now as you move the camera around. ... That looks like the star charts coming into view, now. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Yes. Those are Buzz's two star charts that he is using right now as sun shades over the righthand window, window number 5.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We see the sun shining in through it behind him and plotting out the equatorial - correction, ecliptic plane, and the stars that you're using for the navigation.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. He doesn't really need the charts. He's got them memorized. They're just for show.

speaker: CC
text: We copy.

speaker: LMP
text: While we're pointing up in this direction, we see out our side windows the Sun going by and, of course, out one of our windows right now we've got the Earth. Now right behind my window, of course, we have the Sun, because the Sun is illuminating the star charts that we see. This line represents the ecliptic plane and these lines, vertical lines, represent our reference system that the spacecraft is using at this time. As we approach the Moon, the Moon will gradually grow larger and larger in size and eventually it will

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. We've - Could you attempt a little bit better focus there, 11? Over.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. That's a lot better on the star chart now. We can make out the ecliptic plane and the planets and the Sun and the Moon as they have gone at various places throughout the ecliptic plane. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay, Charlie.

speaker: LMP
text: If we can get some of the wires untangled here, we'll give you a demonstration of how easy pushups are up here.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Roger. Good view of Buzz, there.

speaker: LMP
text: When it gets pretty hard doing it that way, we just roll over and do it the other way.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy. We couldn't figure out whether that was a chinup or a pushup. just take your choice, I guess.

We've got coffee up here in the upper left and various breakfast items, bacon in little small bites, beverages like fruit drink, and over in the center part we have, oh, all kinds of things. Let me pull one out here and see what it is.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

text: Would you believe you're looking at chicken stew, here? All you have to do is - 3 ounces of hot water for 5 or 10 minutes. Now we get our hot water out of a little spigot up here with a

speaker: CC

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP

speaker: CC

speaker: CC

speaker: CMP
text: Well, so much for the food department. I'm going to close up the store down here.

speaker: CC

speaker: CC

speaker: CC

text: Roger, 11. Over.

text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. As the Sun sinks slowly in the west, the White Team bids you good night. If we get a story on the seven-tenths, we can give it to you in about 15 minutes or so; if not, we'll give it to you in the morning. Over.

speaker: LMP

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Over.

text: Okay. Thank you.

text: Roger.

speaker: CC

speaker: CC

speaker: CMP
text: - then we'll get to the waste-water dump - -
