speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. We've got the continent of Africa ... facing toward us right now, and of course, everything's getting smaller and smaller as time goes on. The Mediterranean is completely clear. The Sun looks like it's about to set around Madagascar. The equatorial belt of Africa stands out quite clearly. We're seeing the dark green or a muddy colored green, compared to the sandier colors in the southern tip of Africa and, of course, the Sahara northern coast of Africa. There's a rather remarkable cloud that appears in the vicinity of the border between Afghanistan and Pakistan. It's just about to go into the sunset now. It is casting quite a large shadow. It's isolated. There don't seem to be any other clouds ... the band of clouds near the tropical conversions clouds down around the equator clearly separate the clockwise and the counterclockwise cloud formations. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. We copy your word description on that. I understand you can see a shadow being cast by that cloud over between Afghanistan and Pakistan. Any estimate on how long that shadow would be? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: It looks like it's a shadow. Coming around to - back that way - -

speaker: CC
text: We're getting a lot of background noise now, also. If you will stand by a minute or so until we roll a little further in PTC, I think things will get better.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. It's coming around to the number 1 window. We'll get you ...

speaker: CC
text: Roger, we're hearing you.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. The noise on the COMM seems to have quieted down now. I guess that we've rotated a new antenna into view and probably also the Earth out of view in your window. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. It looks as though the length of the shadow of that cloud is about the same as the width of the Persian Gulf.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. We copy the width of the Persian Gulf, and I guess that all I can give you firsthand is a single isolated data point, and that is that it was clear here in Houston this morning. That's a pretty localized observation. As a result of your waste water dump, it looks like the PTC mode has been disturbed somewhat. We're showing you about 20 degrees out in pitch right now and about 6 degrees in yaw, which is significantly greater, about twice as much - a little more than twice as much as the deviation you had prior to the waste water dump. We' re watching it down here, though, and we'll let you know if we think any corrective action is required. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. Maybe we ought to - next time split that in half, and put half of it on one side and half on the other or something like that.

speaker: CC
text: Yes. We could do that. We were actually pretty interested in seeing what the effect on PTC would be of the waste water dump. We don't recall ever having performed a waste water dump during PTC on previous missions. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Well, now we know.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. I am looking at that cloud now around Pakistan through the sextant, and it appears to be one single cell in the latter stages of development. There is a smaller, more isolated one - -

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We lost you down in the noise on the COMM link here about the time you were describing the single cell cloud formation over Afghanistan-Pakistan area through the sextant. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. It came through a lot clearer through the sextant than with the monocular, and you could definitely tell it was one single cell in the latter stages of development. It must have gone up to over 50,000 feet, though. The eastern Mediterranean is phenomenally clear. You can see all the lakes; the Dead Sea stood out quite well. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. What appears to be the limit of resolution through that sextant from your current position? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Well, I can't see it right now. It's outside the field of view.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: And, I don't know yow you'd really describe the limit of resolution. I will think about that a little.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. I guess the smallest object that you could pick out looking through it would give us a pretty good hack.

speaker: LMP
text: Well, you can see the Nile River going almost up to its source. The lake is obscured by clouds, but you can trace it all the way on up.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: I guess that is down though, isn't it?

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston.

speaker: CMP
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We have been working under the assumption that it would take about an hour for the interference from a waste water dump to dissipate to the point where you could reasonably take star sightings for platform alignment navigation or something of this sort. If you have a spare minute or two, could you comment on the observation condition, now? Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Yes. Stand by one, Bruce.

speaker: CC
text: Okay.

speaker: CMP
text: My guess would be the telescope's probably pretty useless, but you can differentiate in the sextant between water droplets and stars by the difference in their motions.

speaker: CC
text: Okay, Mike. I guess that we've still got - what you are saying is that we've still got a lot of water droplets visible, but you can pick them out and distinguish them in the sextant, then.

speaker: CMP
text: Right. I think so. Buzz is looking through it now. Just a second.

speaker: CC
text: Okay.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. It looks like at this time the sextant would be quite usable for any alignment. There's actually very few ... verticals.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Buzz. How about the telescope? Is it useful now?

speaker: LMP
text: Well, it's not quite as useful; it never seems to be. Depending on the position of the Sun, it's got that band that seems to go across the center. I don't think it's because of the waste water particles that it would lack its effectiveness. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. What - Is this band something that's deposited on the outside of the optics? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: No. I see the reflection from the Sun.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: The Sun bounces off the LM structure. With the LM attached, that telescope is just about useless. Those star charts that MPAD provided us, I think, would be most useful if we had to use the - if for some reason we had to mark through the telescope. We could use those as a guide for what we're looking at and say, "Well, that bright blob over there has got to be that star because that's the position we're in." But so far, we've not been able to pick out any decent star patterns while docked with the LM using the telescope.

speaker: CC
text: This is Houston. We copy.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Go ahead, Apollo 11.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Go ahead - -

speaker: LMP
text: - - How do your read? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We're reading you loud and clear.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. You're coming back a little scratchy. It,looks like our O2 flow transducer's gotten a good bit worse. I just looked at it at the last water accumulator cycling, and it just barely registered - barely crept up above 0.2. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. At the time of your cyclic accumulator stroking, we were on low-bit-rate data, and consequently not receiving the O2 flow parameter. We expect that what you're seeing is probably nominal. That is, it's probably what we would expect from a transducer that's malfunctioning probably in this fashion, and it's just going to keep on getting worse like that. Nothing to worry about. We'll monitor things on the ground here. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. It does look like it's gradually degrading to about zilch.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11 CDR, this is Houston. Radio check. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger, Houston. CDR. Loud and clear.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We're reading you the same. Out.

speaker: CDR
text: And would you check with FAO and see where that errata sheet is? We haven't been able to locate that.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. I understand it's supposed to be the back page in Buzz's operational checklist.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Did you find it? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. We found it.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. And I see you're in P00. If you can give us ACCEPT, we'll uplink a new state vector to you and update the CMC clock. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. You've got it.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. We're through with the uplink. You can go back to BLOCK.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Back to BLOCK.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We woudd like to terminate the charge on battery B at GET of 51 30. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We would like to terminate charging battery Bravo at 51 30 GET. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Terminate charging battery Bravo 51 30.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Out.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. We show you terminating battery B charge. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over

speaker: CDR
text: Go ahead, Houston. Apollo 11.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. We show you terminating battery B charge at about 51 hours 30 minutes. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Out.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. Would you like to have both oxygen and hydrogen purge on? Over.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. Say again. Both what on? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: On the fuel cell purge: would you like to see both oxygen and hydrogen? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Affirmative. We request hydrogen and an oxygen fuel cell purge. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. Any preference which first?

speaker: CC
text: Negative. As long as you've got the H2 purge line heaters on.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. I'll go get - Go ahead with the hydrogen then.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. You copy my NOUN 93?

speaker: CC
text: That's affirmative. We've got it.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. I am going to go ahead and thrust then. Triangle difference is 0.01, but it's sort of difficult at three-tenths rate. I'm required to use medium speed unresolved, and it's difficult to hold the star centered long enough to get a decent mark on it.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy. It looks okay to us.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. I've got the morning news here if you're interested. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Yes, we sure are. We're ready to copy and comment. Isn't that 2:30 there?

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. Go.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. Here we go. The interest in the Flight of Apollo 11 continues at a high level but a competing interest in the Houston area is the easing of watering rules. Mayor Louie Welch promises a lifting of lawn-watering restrictions if the rains continue. Friday is partly cloudy, and there is a 30-percent chance of thunderstorms in the afternoon. In Washington, D.C., the Senate Finance Committee approved extension of the income tax surtax, but a Senate vote on the bill - -

speaker: CMP
text: You cut out, Houston. You cut out.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Where do you hold me cutting out? Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. How do you read now? Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Loud and clear, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: Start after the rains in Houston.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. In Washington, the Senate Finance Committee has approved extension of the income tax surtax, but a Senate vote on the bill currently seemed remote. In Austin, State Representative Ray Lemmon of Houston has been nominated as the National Director of the American Society for Oceanography. Lemmon has proposed a study of the possibility of establishing an institute of oceanography in Texas. This would be the first such institute on the western Gulf of Mexico.

speaker: CC
text: In sports, the Houston Oilers are showing plenty of enthusiasm in their early preseason workouts at Kerrville, and Coach Wally Lemm says he is impressed with the fine group of rookies. National League baseball yesterday, Thursday: St. Louis 11, Philadelphia 3; Montreal 5, over Pittsburg 4; Atlanta 12, Cincinnati 2; San Fransciso 14, and Los Angeles 13. American League: we have Baltimore 3, over Cleveland 2; Detroit 4 to Washington's 3; Minnesota 8 to Chicago 5. Boston at New York was rained out. And in Corby, England, an Irishman, John Coyle has won the world's porridge eating championship by consuming 23 bowls of instant oatmeal in a 10-minute time limit from a field of 35 other competitors. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. I assume Houston didn't play yesterday.

speaker: CC
text: That's correct.

speaker: CMP
text: I'd like to enter Aldrin in the oatmeal eating contest next time.

speaker: CC
text: Is he pretty good at that?

speaker: CMP
text: He's doing his share up here.

speaker: CC
text: Let's see. You all just finished a meal not long ago, too, didn't you?

speaker: LMP
text: I'm still eating.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. Does that - that - -

speaker: CMP
text: He's on his - He's on his 19th bowl.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Are you having any difficulties with gas in the food bags like the 10 crew reported?

speaker: CMP
text: Well, that's intermittently affirmative, Bruce. We have these two hydrogen filters, which work fine as long as you don't hook them up to a food bag. But the entry way into the food bag has enough back pressure to cause the - the filters to start losing their efficiency. A couple of times, I've been tempted to go through that dryout procedure, but we found that simply by leaving the filters alone for a couple of hours, their efficiency seems to be restored.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy.

speaker: CMP
text: Their efficiency ranges anywhere from darn near perfect to terrible just depending on the individual characteristics of the food bags we're putting through them. Some of the food bags are so crimped near the entry-way that there's no way we can work them loose to prevent back pressure.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Hello, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. As you've probably noticed, your coning angle in PTC mode is increased substantially as a result of the waste water dump, the fuel cell purge, and a natural coupling, so it looks like we are going to have to terminate PTC here in a little while. And we'd like to get your feeling as to whether you're still anticipating trying to send back TV signals from inside the LM; and if so, we'll try to provide an attitude that you can hold that'll give us high gain antenna lock on the Earth during the TV and LM activation period. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Yes, we're still planning that activity if the cord lengths work out all right, and we'll accept those attitudes that you work up for us.

speaker: CC
text: This is Houston. Roger. Out.

speaker: LMP
text: When you work up an attitude to get high gain, is there any way that we could get partial Sun in one of the two LM front windows?

speaker: CC
text: This is Houston. We'll have a look at it.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We have a TV attitude for you if you're ready to copy.

speaker: CMP
text: Go ahead. Ready to copy.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. We recommend stopping PTC at GET of 54 45 00, and this should put you at just about the right roll angle. The attitude we recommend is roll 263, pitch 090, yaw 000. This gives you the Earth out of window number 1 in the command module and places the high gain antenna in the CSM window for TV at your convenience. You will also have the Sun shining in - or shining at the hatch on the LM, and if you take down the window shades you should get some sunlight in. We're recommending wide deadband. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. Thank you, Houston. We'll look at that.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Out.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. When we pass the proper roll angle, we're not going to be anywhere near zero degrees yaw. Do you want us to just stop and try until we find ourselves in and then VERB 49 the three angles you gave us?

speaker: CC
text: Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We'd like you to stop at the proper roll angle, then do a VERB 49 to the roll and pitch. Over. Correction, roll and yaw.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Go ahead, 11. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Do you read? Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. Do you read me? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Stand by, Charlie. Yes, we'r going to come out of PTC here at 263 roll and then do VERB 49 to thc recommended attitude.

speaker: CC
text: That sounds fine to us. Ovcr.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Before you open the pressure equalization valve, we'd like the LM/CM DELTA-P. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Let me check it again. It was about 155.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: I read it 158 right now, Charlie.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Thank you much.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. We're stopping PTC at 263 ... 0.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. You're about one-by on this transmission. Say again. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. Do you read?

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. How do you read on the high gain?

speaker: CC
text: 11, how do you read me? Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Read you loud and clear, Charlie. We just switched to HIGH GAIN, and we stopped PTC at roll 263, pitch 90, yaw 0. How do you read?

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Mike. You're five-by now on the high gain. We're right between the 0MNI antennas and pretty horrible COMM on the OMNI's. We got you five-by on the high gain, and we copy the PTC stoppage. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay, fine.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, we're going to open the DIRECT O2 valve and start pumping up the cabin.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Copy.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. We're going to hand over to Goldstone for uplink in about 2 minutes. We might have a momentary dropout of COMM. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Alright. Can you hear our master alarm in the background? That's O2 FLOW HIGH coming through this amplifier.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Copy.

speaker: CMP
text: That photoelectric cell is a good device. It's worked very well.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Say again. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: I say that photoelectric cell amplifier for the master alarm is a good device. It's working very well, and it's a nice pleasing tone.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Copy. Thank you.

speaker: CMP
text: Makes you almost glad to get master alarms.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. As a matter of curiosity, our O2 flow meter is pegged FULL-SCALE HIGH.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. We copy that here. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CMP
text: Boy, that transducer's working somewhat.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We'd like to try to attempt to correlate your O2 flow in transducer with the flow valve that you've got open. How far - How far open would you say you have the REPRESS O2? 0ver. Correction, the DIRECT O2.

speaker: CMP
text: Stand by, Charlie.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay, Charlie. It's not open very far. It's hard to give you a good reading without shunting it again, but the arrow is at about the one o'clock position. Now I reduce the flow, and I'll let it stabilize here. Right now our onboard reading is about 0.4, and that's with the arrow in the O2 valve at the two o'clock position. Would you rather have comparisons of O2 flow readings or would you rather have valve position comparisons?

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: EECOMM's say they'd like to look at valve positions. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Well, we're holding steady now at 0.3 pound per hour, and our cabin pressure is about 54; and I'll close the valve momentarily and then open it again to this position and tell you how much travel is required.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: It's about 30 degrees of travel, Charlie, from the closed position, which is with the arrow pointing at about three to three-thirty, four o'clock.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: Our flow is stabilized now at 0.6.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy. We're reading the same.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CMP
text: Yes, open it back to the one o'clock position.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: Is that enough different positions, or you want more, Charlie?

speaker: CC
text: Mike, that's good - good enough. We're satisfied now. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. We've terminated direct O2, our cabin pressure is 57, and, as a matter of curiosity, when we turn the DIRECT O2 valve OFF, we get a master alarm just like they did in the spacecraft testing.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston, we have a little update for you. When you go into the LM, we'd like you to unstow and bring back to the command module the following items. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Ready to copy.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We'd like you to pick up the - out of the flight data file, the surface checklist, the mission rules NO-GO card, the DPS, APS, RCS limit cue card. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. The reason we wanted you to bring those three items back, we'll have some updates for you, for those three. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. We figured you would.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. We're getting the TV at Goldstone. We're not quite configured here at Houston for the transmission. We'll be up in a couple of minutes. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. This is just for free. This isn't what we had in mind.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. It's a pretty good show here. It looks like you almost got the probe out.

speaker: CMP
text: Yes, it's loose now.

speaker: CDR
text: Can you see that?

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Neil. It's really good.

speaker: CDR
text: Not much light up in that area, but apparently the TV set's able to pick it up.

speaker: CC
text: There are some bright spots shining on the probe. Apparently Sun shafting on it that just gets just about enough for us to make it out. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: I think those are the tunnel lights.

speaker: CC
text: Oh, Okay. You're right.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. It's loose now. Coming down.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Looks like it's a little bit easier than doing that in the chamber.

speaker: CDR
text: You bet. This is the only way ...

speaker: CMP
text: You have to take it easy.

speaker: CDR
text: It's pretty massive, but it goes where you direct it.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. That's a beautiful picture now, we've got. We're looking at a 12-second delay. To us you are just bringing it down by the optics now.

speaker: CDR
text: Mike must have done a smooth job in that docking. There isn't a dent or a mark on the probe.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: We're really getting a great picture here, 11. Over.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. With a 12-foot cable, we estimate you should have about 5 to 6 feet excess when you get the camera into the LM. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: We can see the probe now. Correction, the drogue.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. Drogue removal's coming next.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. As we suspected.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Now it's a good view of the storage area under the couch.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Looks like you're pretty crowded in there with that drogue. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Oh, it's not really bad.

speaker: CMP
text: This TV cable is getting in the way.

speaker: CC
text: We see lots of arms.

speaker: LMP
text: The only problem, Charlie, is these TV stagehands don't know where they stand.

speaker: CC
text: Well, you got to really have a union card, there. We can't really complain too much, I guess.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Do you have a little white dot in the bottom of your monitor - TV monitor? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. We do.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. I guess part of the camera's been burnt out down there. These are really beautiful pictures now, Buzz. Over. Real clear.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. We might have got just a little bit of Sun in there. Is it just one small white dot?

speaker: CC
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: CMP
text: We went up in the tunnel checking the roll angle, Charlie, and it's 2.05 degrees.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Copy. 2.05 on the roll CAL.

speaker: CMP
text: And that's a plus.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Plus.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. The tunnel looks pretty clear to us. Somebody going up there now. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: It's Mike checking his connectors up there now.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. The lighting up in there looks very good to us at this time. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: I think that's mostly the camera. It - it's subdued to say the least.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. It's pretty - It's gathering pretty well to us. We see everything quite clearly up in there.

speaker: CMP
text: Well, the docking latches look good today just like they did yesterday. Everything up in there looks just fine.

speaker: CC
text: That sounds fine to us. Over.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We can even read the decals up there on the LM hatch.

speaker: LMP
text: Well, let me zoom it up and see how much you can read.

speaker: CC
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: We can see the LM umbilical connection quite well there, Buzz. We see you zooming in on one of the decals now. It's, "To reset, unlatch handle; latch behind grip and pull back two full strokes." That's about all we can make out.

speaker: LMP
text: Hey, you get an A-plus.

speaker: CC
text: Thank you very much, sir. At least I passed my eye test.

speaker: LMP
text: I'm standing 6 feet from it, Charlie, and you can read it better than I can. There's something wrong with the system.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: That's a real good view of the LM hatch handle there, 11. 0ver.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger.

speaker: CDR
text: Looks like we'll be ready to go into the LM early if that's okay with you all down there.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. It's fine with us, Neil. Go ahead anytime you wish. Over.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. The white spot you see on your monitor, our TV people say it is a burn spot; but they expect it to dissipate after a couple of hours. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Thank you.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay, the dump valve is actuated.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Copy, 11. We see that very clearly. Is that you, Buzz, with your hand on it?

speaker: CMP
text: Yes.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We're really amazed at the quality of the picture up in the tunnel. It's really superb. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: It is, considering the amount of light up in there.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. We're about to open our hatch now.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. There's that same guy that, when you open up the door, why, he's waiting there for you, and he turns the lights on.

speaker: CC
text: How about that. Just like the refrigerator.

speaker: CC
text: Buzz, the view in through your - by your right - left shoulder there is so good we can see the ascent engine cover, the Velcro on it, and that's about all we can make out right now.

speaker: CC
text: Now we can see the helmet stowage bag - -

speaker: LMP
text: We don't see anything loose up there.

speaker: CC
text: Well, great. Looks good to us. We see the helmet storage bag.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, 11. Houston. We got a view of the PLSS there, off the right of our screen.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Buzz, you already in? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. I'm halfway in, hanging out. Start turning around, I guess.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. We'd like you to read out the LCG reservoir sight level. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: 11, we have a good view of the window there. It looks like the Sun's finally coming through the shade.

speaker: LMP
text: Yes, I'm afraid it's - We're just about plus Z toward the Sun.

speaker: CC
text: That's affirmative. This attitude put both windows right toward the Sun - or the LM. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Well, that may be good in some respects, but -

speaker: CC
text: We had a view, Buzz, of the utility light cord. ...

speaker: LMP
text: Now let me show you a view looking the other way.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. And we see right now the utility light or either the floodlight up there.

speaker: CC
text: I think now I see the utility light still in the stowage bag. Hey, that's a great shot right there. We see you in there. Guess that's Neil and Mike. Better be, anyway.

speaker: CC
text: We see you waving.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. That's really a beautiful shot.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We didn't quite decipher that signal that just came from the CMP.

speaker: LMP
text: Just saying hello. On the LCG sight gage, you got about - oh, it looks like the white mark that's in the plunger is about a quarter to three-eighths inch out into the green away from the red. Is that what you'd like to see? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Stand by. Roger, Buzz. That looks good to us. Thank you much.

speaker: LMP
text: It is the white index, is it not, that you're interested in comparing whether it's in the red or green?

speaker: CC
text: Stand by. That's affirmative, Buzz. It looks good. That's a good reading for us. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: We had a shot moment - a moment ago of the suit disconnect valve.

speaker: LMP
text: I'll open up the windows and see what the lighting condition's going to be like.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. That's a real good view we have of the AOT. You're back now, Buzz, and notice you're taking down one of the window shades. Over.

speaker: CC
text: The light is superb.

speaker: LMP
text: How's the Sun coming in? How's the Sun coming in from this direction going to affect what you can see?

speaker: CC
text: It made it really super. The lighting is excellent in the - in the LM right now. We can make out the AOT, the ISA, and the left-hand window - there's a little glare off of that, but the LMP side the - with the shade down it's really excellent. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Well, let's - I'm turned around, why I took the shade off my side first.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy. The light level for the TV is really excellent. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Yes, the lighting in the LM is very nice now, just like completely daylight; and everything is visible. A good bit lighter than the tunnel was earlier.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We got a good view now, Neil, of the DEDA; and also Buzz's ACA.

speaker: LMP
text: Hey, I'm pointing it at the front hatch now. Everything seems to be in place down there.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, we got the dump valves in view. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We see you removing the ISA now, folding it up, putting it up on the AOT. The instrument panels are coming into view behind.

speaker: LMP
text: Yes, I think it'd probably be best, since we've done SPS burn, to put it back over the instrument panel instead of putting it up over the PLSS on the recharge station. Would you care to comment on that one? We could do either just as easily.

speaker: CC
text: Stand by. We'll have an answer for you momentarily.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. That's really a super shot of the main display.

speaker: LMP
text: The vehicle is surprisingly free of any debris floating around. It's very clean.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. It's pretty hard to describe this view. It's really - really great.

speaker: LMP
text: Now you know how we feel.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. Neil's OPS is about 57, 5800.

speaker: CC
text: Copy.

speaker: LMP
text: And mine's about 5800, also.

speaker: CC
text: Copy.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. That's a good shot of Neil's PLSS, there. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: No, that's mine.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. That moment - a moment ago, we had a good shot of your PLSS, Buzz, and the two helmet stowage bags. Down behind your left shoulder, Buzz, we have the - the DSKY and the ACA.

speaker: LMP
text: We're going to go ahead and take all the Moon data on back into the command module, Charlie.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Buzz, it appears that you're intending to put on the Sun filter and view the Sun through the AOT. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Yes, unfortunately it looks like it's down a little bit more towards ... than I can be able to see in the AOT.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: We got a beautiful view of the side of the command module out of the AOT looking in the left rear detent.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: I can see the hatch and all the - all the EVA handrails. First time we've seen the silvery outside of the command module.

speaker: LMP
text: I can read the letters on the hatch cover. It's a boost cover release; and the big yellow arrow that points toward the opening - place where the tool B goes.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Great shot now back down into the -

speaker: CMP
text: And left on the - -

speaker: CC
text: Go ahead, Buzz. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Say again.

speaker: CC
text: I was just saying we got a great shot looking back into the command module.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. And the left detent, I can see the AO - or the rendezvous radar, and I move to the forward detent and that's about all I've got. I'm looking eyeball to eyeball.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: Charlie, is there any concern about the duration that we ought to have the window shades open?

speaker: CC
text: Stand by.

speaker: LMP
text: We don't have - We don't have any circulation in here, and it might get a little on the warm side.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: We'll - We'll put up a couple of hoses in the command module here and get a little circulation going.

speaker: CC
text: Sounds like a good idea. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. As far as the window shades go in this LM, there's nothing except for crew comfort. I don't think we've got any systems problem. Be sure to put them back up when you egress. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: That we will do.

speaker: LMP
text: Charlie, I'll give you a view out of the overhead window, back looking at the command module right-hand rendezvous window.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Well, we see it now. Thanks a lot, Buzz. That's a good view through the overhead.

speaker: LMP
text: One washer on -

speaker: LMP
text: One washer's on by the overhead.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: There we go. We got it now.

speaker: LMP
text: There wasn't very much debris in the command module or the LM. We found very few loose particles of bolts, nuts, and screws and lint and things. Very few in each spacecraft. They were very clean.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Sounds good.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We have a good view out of the rendezvous - correction, the overhead window of the LM. We don't see anybody staring back at us, though. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Charlie, can you see Mike's two eyeballs staring out through the rendezvous window?

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Stand by. We haven't picked him up yet.

speaker: LMP
text: You are looking through a lot of layers of glass.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We had a - -

speaker: LMP
text: ... on my monitor.

speaker: CC
text: We had a slight glimpse of Mike in the rendezvous window at that time. It's pretty murky looking into there, though.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. Here he is; I've got him. I've got, him on the monitor now.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. We see him staring back at us now. Hello, in there.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Our recommendation for the ISA is to stow it back over the instrument panel. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Will do.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We can make out the markings on the panel. We read SYSTEM A ASCENT FUEL, ASCENT OXIDIZER. Quad 1, quad 4. The - It's really unbelievable, the definition we're getting down here off that little camera. Over.

speaker: CC
text: We can even see the barber pole on the talkbacks.

speaker: CC
text: We can read the markings on the instruments for the glycol pressure, quantity, PCO2. You can even read the scale on the eight ball. Over.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We see the cross-feed barber pole, and we have the Velcro patches back up to the RCS systems now. We can see the markings on the meters, green and red bands, in limits.

speaker: CC
text: We see you raised the cover on the abort stage. We don't recommend that.

speaker: LMP
text: Yes. We're going to tape that one over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: We're going to tape that one over.

speaker: CC
text: We concur.

speaker: LMP
text: The restraints in here do a pretty good job of pulling my pants down.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We haven't quite got that before the 50,000,000 TV audience, yet.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. That's a good view of the eight ball. We see - You can even read the OFF flag, there.

speaker: CC
text: You can see the signal strength meter for the radar, read the numbers on it.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, did you want us to test the cameras in the LM and - I was wondering about that. I saw it in the flight plan, but I'm just wondering if you want to do that on CSM power, or do you want us to take both of the 16mm cameras back in the CSM and test them there? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Stand by, Buzz.

speaker: LMP
text: As an alternative to that, why, we could wait LOI day and do it then when we transfer over to LM power.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Stand by. We'll have an answer.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. On that TV, our commentary - The monitor I was looking at was delayed about 12 seconds, 12 to 15 seconds while it went through our color converter. It was probably - You thought I was crazy, but we were looking at it 15 seconds after you broadcast it. 11, Houston - -

speaker: LMP
text: We understood that, Charlie.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. On the LM cameras, we'd like you to do it on LOI day with the LM power. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. That's what we'll do.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, we're showing you something that came out of the Commander's checklist stowage packet. It's got a 16-millimeter camera in it, and it's got this little cylinder; and I guess - I don't understand what it is. Maybe you can tell us.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Stand by. We can't figure it out either.

speaker: LMP
text: It's got an arrow on the back, and it says "turn," but I'm afraid to turn it.

speaker: CC
text: 11, your friendly geologist says it's the camera cank- crank, excuse me, for the 16-sequence camera if it jams. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: All very well. Thank you.

speaker: LMP
text: There's that word again. The ancillary stowage container.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: The shades couldn't quite hack it, there, Buzz. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, 11. Are you still getting high bit rate off the OMNI's at this distance?

speaker: CC
text: Stand by, Mike.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. About 50 percent of the time, we're getting high bit rate off the OMNI's when you're in PTC. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: You're welcome.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Neil, at this attitude you look like you're about 12 feet long.

speaker: CDR
text: It seems like I always find myself upside-down in whatever I'm doing around here.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Could you give us a few comments on your crew comfort with the CSM hoses moving the air around? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Well, it's picking up a little bit on circulation in here.

speaker: CC
text: What do you estimate the temperature is, Buzz? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Oh, I'd say maybe 73, 75.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: It's hard to tell at this density and pressure of gas, but comfort level is about the - about the same as the command module.

speaker: CC
text: You probably - -

speaker: LMP
text: It was a little warmer or stuffier when we first got in, but it seems to be improving.

speaker: CC
text: Houston copies. Out.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston.

speaker: LMP
text: You may be able to see some - -

speaker: CC
text: Go ahead.

speaker: LMP
text: - - some particles jumping around on your screen. That's just dust particles that are being illuminated by Sun shafting in the window.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. They're very clear now. Over. And that's a good view of Neil's - correction, of Buzz's circuit breaker panel, there.

speaker: LMP
text: I can just barely see the handrail on the front porch from the position on the right-hand window.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Our view of the Panel 11 is - gets brighter, then darker. Are you changing the f-stop at all? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: No, what's happening is, we get pretty close to the window now and then, and it drives the automatic light control into the stop, I think.

speaker: CC
text: I think that's right.

speaker: LMP
text: Yes, I had the switch on OUTSIDE while I was going through the overhead window. That may be what's contributing to some of it.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We seem to be picking up a few more dust particles now. We see them quite clearly in the screen now. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Yes, I'm choking on one every so often.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Your show is going out to the U.S. now. We're about to get the satellite up. It'll be transmitted to some other countries after that. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. I'm checking out this window bracket where I'll be putting it for the EVA pictures of Neil going down the ladder.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. We keep marveling about the color and the clarity of the picture. It's really difficult to describe. It's - It's just perfect. Over.

speaker: CC
text: And, 11, it doesn't look like you're having too much trouble with that bracket up there, Buzz.

speaker: LMP
text: I'll tell you, those new knobs really make it easy to twist the thing and get it cinched down quite tight.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Buzz, how does the alignment look, there?

speaker: LMP
text: It looks pretty good, as well as I can tell without the gear extended. I can't get a real definitive answer, but you couldn't fix it any place to see much more out of the window without hand-holding it for the whole time.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Looks like to us it's going to work real well.

speaker: LMP
text: Give it enough room to - Yes, I think so.

speaker: CC
text: Buzz, we see you putting your window guard in place there, and back up to the ISA now.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, ask FAO if the 90-degree bracket isn't stowed in the Commander's stowage assembly.

speaker: CC
text: Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Buzz, you still looking for that 90-degree bracket? Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Yes, he is looking for it now.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We'll have a word for you in just a moment.

speaker: CDR
text: Our monitor shows pretty good, clear pictures from this angle. I already found the 90-degree bracket.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Neil. It's really a super picture. We've got the ACA, your ACA, the picture of the throttle, the 90-degree bracket. We see your handles, and now over to the bracket.

speaker: LMP
text: That's about the position we'll be putting the camera in after the initial descent on the ladder, and it'll be taken 1 frame a second for most of the EVA.

speaker: CC
text: Houston copies. Out. That's a real good view of that camera.

speaker: LMP
text: Our monitor is a little bit wavy, so it's hard for us to tell when we're - when we've got a steady picture for you.

speaker: CC
text: 11, we have no complaints at all. We don't see that waviness on our picture. It's just really great. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Do the edges of the window look like straight lines to you?

speaker: CC
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. They don't in our monitor, and that leads us to make some corrections to the camera, which probably aren't required sometimes.

speaker: CC
text: Buzz, we have no complaints at all. It's a magnificent picture.

speaker: CC
text: What was that, Buzz, you're chasing now?

speaker: CDR
text: That was - That was me picking up some particles of paint that were floating through the air in front of the camera, there.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Neil. We got it. It appears to us that Neil's about to check the Velcro mat, there.

speaker: CC
text: Okay, Buzz. We see the card up now.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. For those of you that don't know, this is where we log most of our data for each of the LM maneuvers, and we have another card like this that the timeline book that is laid down on the table in front of the data display keyboard; and it's on this timeline that we have all our procedures. But we obviously have to hold these in place in zero g, so we make use of the Velcro patches on the back and on the table so we can attach these down here; and then we just turn the pages over when we go to new sequences in our timeline of procedures.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: And we're ready to copy DOI PAD.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We'll have the FIDO's work that one up for you momentarily.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. That was a good shot of Panel 2. Now we got Panel 3 in view with the TEMP MONITOR switch. The stabilization - station and control panel, we see now, with the MODE CONTROL switches. Now over to the rendezvous radar. Real good.

speaker: CC
text: 11, that's real good camera work.

speaker: LMP
text: That'll be the most unusual position a cameraman's ever had, hanging by his toes from a tunnel and taking the picture upside-down.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Well you're doing a super job. We got a good view of the cross pointer, there. Had a good view of the tape meter.

speaker: LMP
text: We're giving you a picture now of the floor of the cabin. I think you can see the - one of the two portable life support system backpacks here in the center, and on each side, we have the two helmet visors. I'll remove one of them and show you a little closer view of what this looks like.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: Inside the helmet visors are the EVA gloves with the blue tips. I'm about to take those out now.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Buzz. That's a great shot now that we're getting of the helmet, the EVA visor, and also the - the EVA gloves in the background.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. You did say this was going out now, didn't you?

speaker: CC
text: Standby. I think so.

speaker: CC
text: 11, you got a pretty big audience. It's live in the U.S. It's going live to Japan, western Europe, and much of South America. Everybody reports very good color. Appreciate the great show.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Understand. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Buzz, that was a good demonstration of your EVA visor assembly. Appreciate it.

speaker: CC
text: Hey, I like the good view of Mr. Collins down there. We finally see him again.

speaker: CMP
text: Hello there, earthling.

speaker: CC
text: Hello there.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We noticed when you were scanning over Panel 2 a moment ago, 1 and 2, the two eight balls were slightly in disagreement. Control said he'd like a AGS align, there.

speaker: LMP
text: Yes. One of them's AGS, one of them's PNGCS. The problem is, we don't know whether to align AGS to PNGCS or PNGCS to AGS.

speaker: CC
text: Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Chris said he can tell you.

speaker: LMP
text: We'll cage them both.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: Like old home week, Charlie, to get back in the LM again.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. I can imagine.

speaker: CDR
text: The traverse from the bottom of the LM to the aft bulkhead of the command module must be about 16, 20 feet. It's not a disorienting one at all, but it's most interesting to contemplate just pushing off from one and bounding on into the other vehicle all the way through the tunnel.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Must be some experience. Is Collins going to go in and look around?

speaker: CDR
text: We're willing to let him go but he hasn't come up with the price of the ticket yet.

speaker: CDR
text: If I can get him to keep his hands off my DSKY, it'd be a fair swap.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: That's why I've been eating so much today. I haven't had anything to do. He won't let me touch it any more.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. If that's not the Earth, we're in trouble.

speaker: CDR
text: That's the Earth, and we have a very good view of it today. There are a few more cloud bands on than yesterday when we beamed down to you, but it's a beautiful sight.

speaker: CDR
text: We have some horizontal banding in our TV monitor. Are we transmitting that to you, or do you have a clear picture?

speaker: CC
text: Neil, we have a very clear picture. The only thing that we see is a little white dot in the bottom of our screen, which is - our TV guys say is an - apparently a burned out spot in the camera, but it should come back. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. We have that in our monitor also.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We do have three lines across our TV. I thought it was just a transmission problem, but everybody's telling me now that it's probably - it's on the downlink. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: No, those are the same three ones that we have.

speaker: CC
text: Okay.

speaker: LMP
text: How far are - out are we now, Charlie?

speaker: CC
text: Stand by. Give you exact figure.

speaker: CDR
text: Did you notice the difference between yesterday and today? This is as large an image we can - we can give you.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. If you think we're smaller, you're now 177,000 miles out. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Thank you.

speaker: CDR
text: That's nautical miles?

speaker: CC
text: That's affirmative, 11. We -

speaker: LMP
text: ... Hold on.

speaker: CC
text: Go ahead. Over.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We see the - still see the banding along the intratropical convergence. I guess the most predominate one now is around the - up in the - around the equator or slightly north of the equator.

speaker: LMP
text: Yes, that's the way it looks, Charlie. Same as yesterday.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: Just keep the Pacific Ocean nice and clear and calm on splash day, is all we ask.

speaker: CDR
text: And Charlie, I'd like to say hello to all my fellow scouts and scouters at Farragut State Park in Idaho having a National Jamboree there this week; and Apollo 11 would like to send them best wishes.

speaker: CC
text: Thank you, Apollo 11. I'm sure that, if they didn't hear that, they'll get the word through the news, surely appreciate that.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We have you - your subspacecraft point is just off the western coast of South America directly south of about Mexico City. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: That - That looks like what we observe from here.

speaker: CDR
text: And we're going to turn our TV monitor off now for a short bit while we have some other work to do. Apollo 11 signing off.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. Thank you very much. That was one of the greatest shows we've ever seen. We sure appreciate it. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: It was a pleasure.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Could you give us an idea of about how long it will be before you start close - closing the LM back up? Over.

speaker: CDR
text: We've got a little more work to do up here, Charlie. We're going to make sure that we have everything transferred around and stowed the way we want it and try to get a little bit ahead on tomorrow's timeline. I suppose that we could be out of there in another half hour or so if it was necessary.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Neil. We're not trying to push you. We're just trying to get an idea of - about water dumps and starting up the PTC again. Take your sweet time. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. We'd like to get a flight plan update from you for the next couple of hours, here. When you think what the various constraints might be and what - what order you might like us to do things.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Stand by. We'll have that to you in a moment.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Mike, we'd like to go ahead and do a waste-water dump. We'd like you to dump it all the way down to zero. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. We copy that, Charlie.

speaker: CMP
text: How does that work, Charlie?

speaker: CDR
text: Houston, 11.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Did you call? Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. Just noticed that the mast that the EVA light is on is charred brown. It looks as though it took quite a beating during launch.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CDR
text: The EVA light still does work.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We'll let this - the SPAN guys look at this, and we'll be back with you with what we think. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
