text: Roger. And your systems are looking good from down here.

speaker: CMP
text: Yes. Looks good up here too, Bruce.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Go ahead Houston, Apollo 11.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. You are GO for LOI. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. GO for LOI.

speaker: CC
text: And we're showing about 10 minutes and 30 seconds to LOS. I would like to remind you to enable the BD roll on the AUTO RCS switches. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. And confirm you want PCM low going over the hill. Over.

speaker: CC
text: That's affirmative, 11.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: If you want to, I'll put it back to high until just before LOS. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Negative, 11. Low is okay for now. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger.

speaker: CDR
text: Houston, do you want to give me a time check, please?

speaker: CC
text: Roger. I'll give you a Mark at 13 minutes and 30 seconds to ignition.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. And then a GET, please.

speaker: CC
text: Stand by a minute.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: I'll give you a time hack on the GET at 75 hours 37 minutes and I'll try that bias at about a second and a half to allow for the time of flight.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: MARK.

speaker: CC
text: 75 hours 37 minutes GET.

speaker: CDR
text: Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: And I'll give you a time hack on time to ignition at 12 minutes to ignition. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: Stand by for a Mark at TIG minus 12.

speaker: CC
text: MARK.

speaker: CC
text: TIG minus 12.

speaker: CDR
text: You were right on, Bruce. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Out.

speaker: CC
text: Two minutes to LOS.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. All your systems are looking good going around the corner, and we'll see you on the other side. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger.

speaker: CDR
text: Everything looks okay up here.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Out.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston. Do you read? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston. Do you read? Over.

speaker: SC
text: Houston, Apollo 11. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston. We are reading you weakly. Go ahead. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. Burn status report follows. DELTA-TIG zero, burn time 557, ... VGX minus O.1, VGY

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. These residuals, do you have minus 0.1?

speaker: SC
text: ... VGX minus 0.1, VGY minus 0.1, VGZ 1.1, and a burn time of 5 plus 57. Stand by, maybe the COMM will improve a little bit. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Are you in the process of acquiring data on the burn? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston. How do you read?

speaker: CDR
text: Reading you loud and clear, Houston. How us?

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Reading you the same, now. Could you repeat your burn status report? We copied the residuals and burn time, and that was about it. Send the whole thing again, please.

speaker: CDR
text: It was like - like perfect! DELTA-TIG zero, burn time 557, shaft value on the angles, VGX minus 0.1, VGY minus 0.1, VGZ plus 0.1, no trim, minus 6.8 on DELTA-VC, fuel was 38.8, LOX 39.0, plus 50 on balance, and we ran an increase on the PUGS, NOUN 44 showed us in a 60.9 by 169.9.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy your burn status report. And the spacecraft is looking good to us on telemetry.

speaker: CDR
text: Everything looks good up here.

speaker: CDR
text: Apollo 11 is getting its first view of the landing approach. This time we are going over the Taruntius crater, and the pictures and maps brought back by Apollo 8 and 10 have given us a very good preview of what to look at here. It looks very much like the pictures, but like the difference between watching a real football game and watching it on TV. There's no substitute for actually being here.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We concur, and we surely wish we could see it firsthand, also.

speaker: LMP
text: We're going over the Messier series of craters right at the time, looking vertically down on them, and Messier A we can see good sized blocks in the bottom of the crater. I don't know what our altitude is now, but in any case, those are pretty good size blocks.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. Just roughly, it looks like you are about 120 miles or 13O miles right now - make that 127 miles.

speaker: CDR
text: We're approaching PDI point now. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: There's Secchi in sight.

speaker: LMP
text: We're going over Mount Marilyn at the present time, and it's ignition point.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Thank you. And our preliminary tracking data for the first few minutes shows you in a 61.6 by 169.5 orbit. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: And Jim is smiling.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. During your SPS burn as played back on tape down here, we've observed the nitrogen tank Bravo pressure in the SPS system dropping a little bit more than we anticipated. It's holding steady right now. We'll continue to watch it and keep you posted if anything comes up. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Right. And it has held steady - -

speaker: CDR
text: Currently going over Maskelyne Mas -

speaker: CDR
text: Okay.

speaker: CDR
text: And Boothill, Duke Island, Sidewinder, looking at Maskelyne W, that's the yaw round checkpoint, and just coming into the terminator. At the terminator it's ashen and gray. As you get further away from the terminator, it gets to be

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. We're recording your comments for posterity.

speaker: CDR
text: (Laughter) Okay.

speaker: CMP
text: Did somebody in the background - do they accuse us of being compromisers? Huh!

speaker: CDR
text: And landing site is well into the dark here. I don't think we're going to be able to see anything of the landing site this early.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. When you have a free minute, could you give us your onboard readout of N2 tank Bravo, please. And we'd like to make sure you understand that ever since you stopped thrusting with the SPS, the temperature in this tank has remained steady. Over. Make that the pressure has remained steady.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. We understand tank pressure has stayed steady. Thank you.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. We're showing the N2 tank pressure and the tank Bravo to he 1960, something like that, and Alfa is, oh, about 2250. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We show 2249 in Alfa and 1946 down here.

speaker: LMP
text: All right.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. How about coming up with some roll, pitch, and yaw angles in which to stop this so called ORB RATE that I'm doing.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Standby.

speaker: CC
text: We'll have them for you in a minute, 11.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. And time to stop also, please.

speaker: CC
text: Yes, indeed.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We show you, in the flight plan, staying in orbital rate until about 79 hours 10 minutes. Do you have some particular attitude or reason for wanting to go inertial? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: No, that's fine. I just wanted to confirm that. Until 79 10, then we'll breeze around here in orbit.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. And we've got an observation you can make if you have some time up there. There's been some lunar transient events reported in the vicinity of Aristarchus. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. We just went into spacecraft darkness. Until then, why, we couldn't see a thing down below us. But now, with earthshine, the visibility is pretty fair. Looking back behind me, now, I can see the corona from where the Sun has just set. And we'll get out the map and see what we can find around Aristarchus

speaker: CDR
text: We're coming upon Aristarchus right now - -

speaker: CC
text: - - Okay. Aristarchus is at angle Echo 9 on your ATO chart. It's about 394 miles north of track. However, at your present altitude, which is about 167 nautical miles, it ought to be over - that is within view of your horizon: 23 degrees north, 47 west. Take a look and see if you see anything worth noting up there. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Both looking.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Out.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, 11. It might help us a little bit if you could give us a time of crossing of 45 west.

speaker: CC
text: Say again, please, 11.

speaker: LMP
text: You might give us a time of crossing of 45 west, and then we'll know when to start searching for Aristarchus.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. You'll be crossing 45 west at 77 04 10 or about 40 seconds from now. Over. Thirty seconds from now.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, when we lose the S-band, we'd like to get 0MNI Charlie from you. And update my last, that 77 04 was the time when Aristarchus should

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. That sounds better because we just went by Copernicus a little bit ago.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We show you at about 27 degrees longitude right now.

speaker: LMP
text: Righto.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, when a star sets up here, there's no doubt about it. One instant it's there, and the next instant it's just completely gone.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We request you use OMNI Charlie at this time. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. Going to OMNI Charlie.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Out.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Seems to me since we know orbits so precisely, and know where the stars are so precisely, and the time of setting of a star or a planet to so very fine a degree, that this might be a pretty good means of measuring the altitude of the horizon ...

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: Hey, Houston. I'm looking north up toward Aristarchus now, and I can't really tell at that distance whether I am really looking at Aristarchus, but there's an area that is considerably more illuminated than the surrounding area. It just has - seems to have a slight amount of fluorescence to it. A crater can be seen, and the area around the crater is quite bright.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. We copy.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. Looking up at the same area now and it does seem to be reflecting some of the earthshine. I'm not sure whether it was worked

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. Can you discern any difference in color of the illumination, and is that an inner or an outer wall from the crater? Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. That's an inner wall of the crater.

speaker: LMP
text: No, there doesn't appear to be any color involved in it, Bruce.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. You said inner wall. Would that be the inner edge of the northern surface?

speaker: CMP
text: I guess it would be the inner edge of the westnorthwest part, the part that would be more nearly normal if you were looking at it from the Earth.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Have you used the monocular on this? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Stand by one.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Like you to know this quest for science has caused me to lose my E memory program, it's in here somewhere, but I can't find it.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. We're - we're hearing only a partial COMM. Say again please.

speaker: CDR
text: I think ...

speaker: CDR
text: Houston, we will give it a try if we have the opportunity on next - when we are not in the middle of lunch, and trying to find the monocular.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Copied you that time. Expect in the next REV you will probably be getting ready for LOI 2.

speaker: CC
text: So, let's wind this up, and since we've got some other things to talk to you about in a few minutes. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. We're targeting - planning to make the LOI 2 burn now using bank A only. We'll have the PAD and everything for you next time around. Just trying to economise a little on bank B. Bank B is holding, though.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. Understand.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. In order to improve the communications a little bit here, we'd like to try to get you on the high gain antenna. We're recommending a pitch angle of 0, yaw 355 - I say again 355, the track switch to MANUAL, and wide beamwidth. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. You ready to switch to high gain now?

speaker: CC
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Do you read?

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. We read you. It seems to be rather marginal on the high gain.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We concur.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. Could you give us a time of crossing the prime meridian 150 west? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Stand by about a half a second, here. Okay. Your time of crossing the 150 west meridian will be 77 50 05. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. We have about 6 minutes remaining until LOS, and in order that we may configure our ground lines, we'd like to know if you're still planning to have the TV up with the beginning of the next pass. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger, Houston. We'll try to have it ready.

speaker: CC
text: This is Houston. We are inquiring if it is your plan to. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Houston. Roger. Out.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: For use in connection with the prime meridian crossing, you have an orbital period now of 2 hours 8 minutes and 37 seconds. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Out.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. A little over 2 minutes to LOS. All your systems parameters and orbit are looking good from the ground. We have AOS on the other side at 78 23 31. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. That was 31 on the end.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: This is Apollo 11. Are you picking up our signals okay?

speaker: LMP
text: - - No, no, no - -

speaker: CC
text: - - the bottom of the picture. I guess that's the spot on the tube.

speaker: LMP
text: I'm sorry about that one.

speaker: CC
text: And if you give us P00 and ACCEPT, we will uplink our new state vector and target load to you.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. One of the larger craters on the back side - I noticed a small, dark speck on the outer wall and I put the monocular on it. I was able to see - oh, an area maybe a quarter of a mile in diameter. It was really a freshlooking dark colored pit, and that seems to be in contrast with all the other fresh little craters or holes that you can perceive on the walls of any of these craters. Around this particular one there seems to be two or three of these - especially the one that caught my attention. Quite remarkable. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Do you have a location on that one?

speaker: LMP
text: No, not a precise one. I've got several pictures of it, though.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy.

speaker: CC
text: We're getting a beautiful picture in down there now, 11. The color's coming in quite clearly, and we can see the horizon and the relative blackness of space, and without getting into the question of grays and browns, it looks, at least on our monitor, sort of a brownish gray.

speaker: LMP
text: That's a good, reasonable way of describing it. It appears to me as though it made a difference just sitting back in the tunnel and gazing at all windows; it makes a difference which one you're looking out of. For example, the camera

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: And if you rear back 95 or 100 degrees ...

speaker: MS
text: ... Still holding ... Okay.

speaker: CC
text: Say again, 11?

speaker: LMP
text: I'd say we're about 95 degrees east, coming up on Smyth's Sea.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. And for your information, we show you at an altitude of about 92 miles above the surface right now.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. Could you observe a difference in the N2 pressures before LOI? It seems to me as though the two were not equal on the ... B tank was a little low on pressure. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: I'm flying it in SPS minimum impulse, Houston, and it's rather difficult to keep it on a constant data. The LM wants to wander up and down. I'm not sure if it's in response to MASCONN's or what, but I can get it completely stabilized in DATA and let it alone, and in another couple of minutes it will have developed its own rate.

speaker: CC
text: This is Houston. Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, we'll be moving shortly from the side window to the hatch window, and we'll try and pick up some of the landmarks that we'll be looking at as we approach the powered descent. Over.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. Roger. And we're through with the uplinks; the computer is yours. You can go to BLOCK and we'll have the information on nitrogen for you shortly. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. Copy.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay, Houston. Several minutes ago I was exactly steady on data, and since then I have been moving

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: We're over Smyth's Sea right now.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: We're about 88 degrees east, I would estimate.

speaker: CC
text: We show you about south of the - southwest of the crater Jansky right now.

speaker: CMP
text: Smyth Sea doesn't look much like a sea. It - The area which is devoid of craters, of which there's not very much, is sort of a hilly looking area. It's not like the maria at all.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy that about the sea, and it looks like you were just giving us a view of the crater Neper, the large crater on the left, and Jansky on the right.

speaker: CMP
text: We think you're close, but no cigar.

speaker: CC
text: 11, this is Houston. Would you care to comment on some of these craters as we go by?

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. We're approaching the approach path to ignition. This is equivalent to 13 minutes before ignition, and we're at about 83 degrees, I guess - 83 degrees east. That correspond to location you're holding there presently?

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We're showing your present position as about 77 - 76 degrees east looking back towards the east.

speaker: CMP
text: Hey, you should be looking back at Smyth Sea now.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, what you're seeing in the middle of the screen now is the crater Schubert and Gilbert U is in the center right now; and this comes up at about - a little over 12 minutes before power decent. Instead of me looking - Instead of looking back at it, we'd be looking straight down at it in descent.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: And we show you at an altitude now of about 110 miles; and, of course, you'll be considerably lower at the initiation of powered descent.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay, Houston. Look at register 3 on the DSKY data. This data is increasing toward my desired of 315; and I'll let the hand controller alone here, and I'll bet you it reverses itself.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. We're watching the DSKY now, and it's still coming in beautifully on the TV.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. There's - on the right side of the screen at the present time, there's a triple crater with - with a small crater between the first and second; and the one at the bottom of the screen is Schubert Y. Zoom in; it does have a central peak in Schubert Y. Actually, several of them, and you can observe those plus the rim craters at the bottom of your screen.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We're seeing the central peak quite clearly now.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. We're zooming in now on a crater called Schubert N. Schubert N, very conical inside walls and the bottom appears to be nearly flat.

speaker: CMP
text: Look at data on the DSKY. It's stabilized and is holding steady now.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: Looking out the window I can see a number of small craters on the bottom of Schubert N.

speaker: CMP
text: We're coming up on the Foaming Sea where I'll be doing some P22 marking on a crater of my choice, name of crater, Camp.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. We'll be watching for Neper.

speaker: CMP
text: And notice register 3 has reversed itself, and it's heading back the other way now without any pitch thruster firing.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Mike. We confirm that you've changed the direction of your pitch rate.

speaker: CMP
text: Generally speaking - -

speaker: LMP
text: The crater - -

speaker: CMP
text: - - The tendency seems to be to pull the LM down toward the center of the Moon there as in a gravity gradient experiment.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. We copy - -

speaker: CMP
text: It may have something to do with MASSCON's or it may - -

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy ...

speaker: CMP
text: It may have something to do with MASSCON's or it may just be the peculiarity of the DSKY display.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. We've observed the behavior of your DSKY, and I think we've got the data here to work on it. Let us grind around a little while on it, and we'll report back to you, probably in a REV or two.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Well, in the meantime, I'm going to pitch down toward 315.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: Three craters - three horizontal craters that you now have in the field of view are immediately underneath the ground track. The right hand is the largest crater that you see, Dubiago P.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We concur on the identification of that crater.

speaker: CC
text: And we show you coming up on landmark Alfa 1 here shortly.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Mike's having his first look at Alfa 1 at the present time.

speaker: CMP
text: Yea. It's a very bright crater. It's not a large one but an extremely bright one. It looks like a very recent and, I would guess, impact crater with rays streaming out in all directions which should make my - Correction - the Foaming Sea easy to see coming up on it now. Crater Camp is one of the smaller ones out on the - on the floor of the Foaming Sea.

speaker: CC
text: Here we show you over the Sea of Fertility now, and we ought to have Langrenus down south of track a few degrees, about 9 degrees south of track.

speaker: LMP
text: Now the crater that's in the center of the screen now is Webb. We'd be looking straight down on it at about 6 minutes before power descent. It has a relatively flat bottom to the crater, and you can see maybe two or three craters that are in the bottom of it on the western wall, the wall that's now nearest the - the camera. Near the bottom of the screen, we can see a dimple crater, just on the outside. And then coming back toward the bottom of the screen and to the left, you can see a series of depressions. It's this type of connected craters that give us most interest to discover why they're in the particular pattern that they're in. I'll zoom the camera in now and try and give you a closer look at it.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We're observing the dimple crater now. The central peak we can see on the Orbiter photos doesn't seem to stand out very well here.

speaker: LMP
text: Well, they're not central peaks. They're depressions in the center.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: And you'll notice on the pitch thruster activity, I've still - I've put in a dozen mininum impulses in pitchdown, and I'm still far from correcting back to 315.

speaker: LMP
text: We're moving the camera over to the right window now to give you Langrenus, its - its several central peaks and -

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We got Langrenus in our screen now.

speaker: CC
text: Okay, 11. This is Houston. We're getting a beautiful picture of Langrenus now with its rather conspicuous central peak.

speaker: CMP
text: The Sea of Fertility doesn't look very fertile to me. I don't know who named it.

speaker: CDR
text: Well, it may have been named by a gentleman whom this crater was named after, Langrenus. Langrenus was a cartographer to the King of Spain and made one of the - one of the early reasonably accurate maps of the Moon.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. That's very interesting - -

speaker: CDR
text: ... at least it sounds better for our purposes than the Sea of Crises.

speaker: CC
text: Amen to that.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. It looks like you're coming inside now on the camera.

speaker: LMP
text: Well, I can't get behind to see the monitor. I'll bring the focus in, but we're going to be looking down past one of the LM quads and one of the antennas almost straight down at the ground track that we'll be seeing coming in now. I guess there's maybe 2 or 3 minutes before power descent.

speaker: LMP
text: All right, that should put the LM structure about in focus, and I'm going to move it out to infinity and then expand the field of view.

speaker: LMP
text: Crater Secchi is out my window now, window number 2.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Apollo 11. This is Houston. We show you coming up on the terminator at 78 53, about 7 minutes from now, and we've also got the LOI 2 and TEI 5 PAD's ready for you after the TV whenever you want to terminate. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: And we're getting a good view of the track leading into the landing site now and -

speaker: CC
text: Okay, And it looks like we got Secchi K, went by about 10 seconds ago; coming up on Apollo Ridge.

speaker: CC
text: And in the right hand portion of our screen right now, we can see Messier Alfa and Bravo with the light colored rays streaming off in one direction.

speaker: LMP
text: I don't know if you can make out, but in the Sea of Fertility there are a number of craters that are just barely discernible, old, old craters whose outlines are just barely able to be seen.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. I think we can make them out. The color really enhances our ability to discern features and craters over what we see in real time on our black and white monitor.

speaker: LMP
text: Right. The - At these low Sun angles, there's no trace of brown, it's now returned to a very gray appearance and, like the 8 crew says, it has a look of plaster of paris to it at this Sun angle, which is completely lacking in ...

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. This is very close to ignition point for power descent. Just passing Mount Marilyn that - that triangular shaped mountain that you see in the center of the screen at the present time with crater Secchi Theta on top of the far northern edge of the mountain.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We're getting a good view of Mount Marilyn and the Secchi Theta.

speaker: LMP
text: And now we're looking at what we call Boot Hill; occurs 20 seconds into the descent.

speaker: LMP

speaker: CC

speaker: CC
text: Eagle, this is Houston coming through the 210. How do you read? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Read you loud and clear.

speaker: CC
text: Eagle, this is Houston. We're happy with all our data in all modes. You can power down the COMM now. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. I understand. Eagle will power down the COMM, and we are just approaching 27 volts now. It looks like we won't have to bother with the high taps.

speaker: CC
text: Right.

speaker: LMP
text: We're powering down. Out.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Copy. Out.

speaker: CC
text: Columbia, this is Houston. We got a TEI 11 PAD for you and an update on the water dump. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Stand by one, Houston. Are you through with the DSKY?

speaker: CC
text: That's affirmative. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Columbia. Ready to copy TEI 11. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Columbia. Here we come with the TEI 11. SPS G&N: 37200, minus 060, plus 047. NOUN 33, 098 05 2422, plus 41448, plus 03719, minus 02422. Roll is NA, pitch 020, the rest of the PAD is NA. Set stars are NA. The ullage is two quads -

speaker: CMP
text: All right. I read back: TEI 11, SPS G&N: 37200, minus 060, plus 047, plus 098, 05 2422, plus 41448, plus 03719, minus 02422; NA, 020; the rest of the PAD NA. Ullage, two jets for 16 seconds, Quads B and D. Undocked present CSM weight is okay in the DAP.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. And we'd like you to do a waste water dump at 84 hours down to 25 percent. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. I understand. Waste water dump to 25 percent at 84 hours.

speaker: CMP
text: Good idea.

speaker: CMP
text: I'm in REACQ and NARROW now.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Also, that water that you got on the aft bulkhead, we - If it's not too much, we just recommend sopping it up and then throwing the sponges away in the waste stowage area. If it's too much, then we recommend using the procedure in the checklist on page F10-14. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: All right. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Would you have Buzz make sure he gives us the OPS pressure readings before you close up? Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Will do.

speaker: CDR
text: Houston, 11. The OPS read 5750, both bottles.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Roger. Reading you fine, and it looks like the automatic REACQ went very well just as soon as you came around the limb. We have several small items to discuss with you here just before you go to sleep. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Go ahead. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Okay, 11. First of all, on our LM systems checks, everything went fine. I would like to remind you, though, tomorrow you may see an ascent pressure light when you activate the MC&W. There should be no problem, however. You did note that the APS AUX tank pressure was only reading 111 psi, which is normal at this point, but below the level which will trigger your light due to the helium which has been dissolved into the propellant. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. Understand that. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. And next item, the supercritical helium rise rate is nominal, and you also had that question for us about your thruster activity during the P22 on the last REV. Believe we understand that now, as you reported that your pitch was in ACCEL COMMAND and your yaw and roll were in RATE COMMAND. You were firing your pitch thrusters. This will couple rates into your yaw and roll axes, and the - You were at that time holding only half a degree deadband and coupling rates into yaw and roll produced the extra firings about the yaw and roll axes. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Yes. That may be true. It's very peculiar coupling, in that it waits longer than you would think and its reaction is greater than you would think. We were getting yaw rates of around four tenths of a degree per second, for example.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Mike. We did play the data back, and that's the way it looked upon analysis of the chart recordings back here. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Fine.

speaker: CC
text: They've also looked at the results of your landmark tracking. The marks all apparently were very good, and we've got a full page of data here relative to the altitudes of the various site locations, which I won't read up to you, but I did want to let you know that the marks apparently went very well. I also have your consumable budgets, particularly your RCS propellant quantities. They're Deltas from nominal if you should want them. Your worst quad is quad Charlie, which is 9 percent low. I'll not read up the others unless you want them. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. How about the O2 fuel cell purge? You want that now?

speaker: CC
text: I'll have to stand by just a moment.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. And then the other one is, we're still charging battery A.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We would like to delay the fuel cell purge until the backside of the Moon, and you go ahead and - should terminate your battery charge at this time. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. Understand. I knew we had another O2 and H2 purge coming up in the morning; I wasn't sure whether you wanted to go through with this one or not. I'll wait until the next side and then do it.

speaker: CC
text: That's fine, Buzz.

speaker: LMP
text: Terminate battery charging now.

speaker: CC
text: That's right, and one other systems item here - in order to balance your CRYO tanks, would you get your O2 tank 1 and your H 2 tank 2 heaters off? Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. I have O2 tank heater 1 off, and H2 tank heater 2 off.

speaker: CC
text: That's right, Mike, and we believe you have your quad Bravo and quad Charlie turned off in your DAP at this time, and a 5 degree deadband. We'd prefer a 10 degree deadband for your sleep period overnight here. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: One other item relative to a malfunction procedure. It's unlikely that you'll have to worry about this

speaker: CMP
text: Understand, and note has been made in my checklist.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Roger. That just about takes care of all the items we have here on the ground before time to hit the sack, and I guess you will have a presleep check for us before you go to bed.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. We're in the midst of cycling the O2 and H2 fans now.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: And the radiation is as follows: CDR 11012, CMP 100l3, LMP 09015. Negative medication. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Copy, 11.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. We're thinking about taking the monocular with us on into the LM. We think it might prove to be of some use. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Buzz. It sounds like a good idea for some of your surveying work there inside the cockpit. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. You want to run that by with whoever might be concerned?

speaker: CC
text: I sure will.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. We have apparently lost the high gain lock. We would appreciate it if you would give us a help manually to try to relock up on the high gain. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. ..

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Reading you very weak, still too far down in the noise to complete the full transmission. If you'd give us a hand on a manual relock, we'd appreciate it.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. We're still unable to pick you up on the high gain antenna. Request you go to MANUAL, and wide beamwidth. The pitch and yaw angles in your checklist are good ones. You should be able to find us there. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. How do you read now?

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Loud and clear this time. How me?

speaker: LMP
text: Loud and clear. You faded out on your last transmission. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Are you in wide beam now?

speaker: LMP
text: Negative. I got you locked back on again REACQ and narrow.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. That's all we want. We want to stay in narrow, and we're a little puzzled about why we lost you here a few minutes ago. Do you have any ideas?

speaker: LMP
text: No, we sure don't (cough) - sure don't. We're showing - we're showing about 15 degrees plus pitch and about 270. That ought to be good and clear.

speaker: CC
text: We concur there. We still don't have any good ideas on why we were lost then.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Would you confirm that we did acquire automatically when you came around the limb for this passage. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: That's confirmed.

speaker: CC
text: Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. On your AUTO RCS SELECT switches, we show quad Bravo disabled but quad Charlie only partially disabled. Charlie 3, I believe, is the only one you have selected off. Is that correct?

speaker: CMP
text: Yes. Roger. That's correct.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: How do they look to you now, Houston?

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We see them all disabled at this time. Thank you.

speaker: CMP
text: Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We're going to try to check out this ability to automatically reacquire on the S band, and what we want to do is to secure our uplink carrier for about 30 seconds. Then we will turn it back on and see if the spacecraft equipment will automatically reacquire. So if you do not get a call from us within about 3 minutes, that means we have not been able to reacquire and request your assistance on a manual acquisition. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. We understand.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We also would appreciate - if you will note the angles that the antenna tracks through in its attempt to reacquire. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. We'll do that.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. It looks like we're locked back up again with no delay. How does it look on board? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. The signal strength dropped very rapidly to zero; and the pitch and yaw, in about 3 secconds, moved toward 40 degrees pitch and 240 degrees yaw. Right now, they're sitting on about 15 degrees pitch and about 265 degrees yaw. So they didn't move very far, about 30 degrees apiece; and then they picked right back on up again. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Some of "The Luckiest People" in the background there. We copied your pitch and yaw angles.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Could you give us the location of your - pitch and yaw location of your position indicators? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. They're in the same position as the antenna right now; plus 15 degrees pitch and - no, now wait a minute. I got them - got it at about 275 instead of 265.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We'd like to try the same procedure once more. We'll leave the carrier a little longer and be back up for a call within 4 minutes. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We're locked back up again. Can you give us a report on how the antenna behaved?

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. It was essentially identical as before. The pitch went to 45, 40 to 45 and the yaw went to about - to about 255, 245 to 255; and then it rather quickly locked up at 15 degrees pitch and 270 yaw. Over.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Roger. Your angles are 45 and 255. Do I understand that as soon as the carrier dropped, it went to these angles; or did it only go to these angles after the uplink carrier was reenabled and the antenna began to reacquire? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: No. As soon as the carrier dropped off, why, it drifted over into those angles and stayed there. Then when it came back up again, why, it hunted around for a while, but it didn't get any further off. Gradually brought it on in to the angles where it is right now; and then the signal strength would take several jumps as evidently it goes from wide to medium to narrow. Over.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Understand. And on another subject, request you zero your optics for the night. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Zeroed.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Can you confirm that you have changed the CO2 filter as per flight plan in the last hour? Over?

speaker: CMP
text: No. We're still eating. We're about to do it. We'll let you know.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11. And we've got about 14 minutes until LOS. A0S is 86 30, an hour away. We're wondering whether or not you plan to have one man up at that time or would you all like to be asleep inside the next hour? Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Somebody will be up.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. The thing that we're still puzzling on is the antenna, and if - as long as there will be somebody up, why, we would like to have somebody check the automatic REACQ on the next AOS.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. We'll do that. We haven't chlorinated the water yet, and we haven't changed the lithium hydroxide. We're just still finishing up dinner.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Mike. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. We have LOS coming up in 2 minutes now, and A0S will be at 86 plus 28 plus 15. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: We'll see you on the other side, Houston.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. Over.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Loud and clear here. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. We just appeared to get a solid lock for the last - oh, about a minute. The ... needle's been wandering up and down, and the pitch and yaw needles have been wandering around, but it appears to have reacquired by itself solidly now. We're just finishing up our fuel cell purge. Hydrogen on number 3 is the last to go off. It'll be coming off in just a second.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, 11.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. We believe we've tracked down the reacquisition problem we had on the previous REV. It looks like it was a receiver power supply here on the ground and no problems in the spacecraft at all. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Glad to hear it.

speaker: CC
text: 11, that really winds things up as far as we're concerned on the ground, for the evening. We're ready to go to bed and get a little sleep. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Yes. We're about to join you.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11. Good morning from the Black Team.

speaker: CMP
text: Good morning, Houston.

speaker: CC
text: Good morning. We got about 2 minutes to LOS here, Mike.

speaker: CMP
text: ... You guys wake up early.

speaker: CC
text: (Laughing) Yes, you're about 2 minutes early on the wakeup. Looks like you were really sawing them away.

speaker: CMP
text: You're right.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. For planning purposes, you can go ahead and take the monocular into the LM with you.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. I'll tell them. How are all the CSM systems looking?

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. Looks like the command module's in good shape. Black Team has been watching it real closely for you.

speaker: CMP
text: We sure appreciate that. Because I sure haven't.

speaker: CC
text: Say again.

speaker: CMP
text: I say because I sure have not.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11. Thirty seconds. AOS will be 94 plus 21.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Standing by.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Go.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. How do you read the BIOMED in the LMP with the LCG on? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Stand by, 11.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. We have good data on all 3 crewmen. No. Belay that. The Commander we do not have yet.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. He's not up yet.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. We just had a very good view of the landing site. We can pick out almost all of the features we've identified previously.

speaker: SC
text: Stand by.

speaker: LMP
text: Stand by a little, please.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We're standing by. And that's the block data on the maneuver PAD, by the way.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11 is a couple of minutes away from this rolling right 40 degrees to roll 122, pitch 229, yaw 0. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Roger. We're standing by.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. Ready to copy.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Apollo 11, Houston. Here's your block data, TEI 30. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Ready to copy.

speaker: CC
text: SPS/G&N: 36639; your NOUN 48, minus 072, plus 051; your NOUN 33, 135 24 4000; NOUN 81, plus 32178, plus 06036, minus 01304, your pitch 064. The rest is NA. Ullage: two jet, 16 seconds; and it's based on L0I REFSMMAT. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. TEI 30 SPS/G&N: 36639 minus 072, plus 051, 135 24 4000, plus 32178, plus 06036, minus 01304, pitch 064, two jets 16 second, LOI REFSMMAT. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Readback correct. Your consumables update?

speaker: CMP
text: Yes. Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. GET 91 plus 30, minus 7 percent; Alfa minus 8, Bravo minus 2.5, Charlie minus 10, Delta minus 6.5. H2 total, minus 2 pounds; oxygen total, plus 9 pounds. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Thank you. And on board, we're reading for quad Alfa 75 percent, Bravo 78, Charlie 78, and Delta 77 percent.

speaker: CC
text: 11, Houston. We copy.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. I have your base line altitude update now, if Buzz is ready to copy.

speaker: CMP
text: Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Alfa 1 is 500, that's 500 feet above the landing site. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Alfa 1 is 500 feet above the landing site. Thank you.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. Our crew status report for sleep: CDR 5.5, CMP 6.0, LMP 5.0. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Roger. We have that now.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Apollo 11. Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. The "Black Bugle" just arrived with some morning news briefs if you're ready.

speaker: CDR
text: Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. Church services around the world today are mentioning Apollo 11 in their prayers. President Nixon's worship service at the White House is also dedicated to the mission, and our fellow astronaut, Frank Borman, is still in there pitching and will read the passage from Genesis which was read on Apollo 8 last Christmas. The Cabinet and members of Congress, with emphasis on the Senate and House space committees, have been invited, along with a number of other guests. Buzz, your son, Andy, got a tour of MSC yesterday. Your Uncle Bob Moon accompanied him on the visit which included the LRL. Among the - -

speaker: LMP
text: - - Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Among the large headlines concerning Apollo this morning, there's one asking that you watch for a lovely girl with a big rabbit. An ancient legend says a beautiful Chinese girl called Chang-o has been living there for 4000 years. It seems she was banished to the Moon because she stole the pill of immortality from her husband. You might also look for her companion, a large Chinese rabbit, who is easy to spot since he is always standing on his hind feet in the shade of a cinnamon tree. The name of the rabbit is not reported.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. We'll keep a close eye out for the bunny girl.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. You residents of the spacecraft Columbia may be interested in knowing that today is Independence Day in the country of Colombia. Gloria Diaz of the Philippines was crowned Miss Universe last night. She defeated 60 other girls for the global beauty title. Miss Diaz is 18, with black hair and eyes, and measures 34-1/2, 23, 34-1/2. First runner up was Miss Australia, followed by Miss Israel, and Miss Japan. While you're on your way back Tuesday night, the American and

speaker: CDR
text: Thank you very much. We appreciate the news.

speaker: LMP
text: Black Team, we'll be looking for an interesting day with you all tomorrow.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We'll be going off here shortly, and we'll pick you up in the morning for sure.

speaker: CC
text: Apollo 11, Houston. Three minutes to LOS; AOS at 96 plus 20.

speaker: CDR
text: Apollo 11. 96 20. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Columbia. Houston. Do you read? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Hello, Houston, this is Eagle. How do you read? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Eagle, this is Houston. Are you calling? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. How do you read? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Reading you about three by, Buzz; a lot of noise on the loop. We think it's coming from Columbia, but we can't tell. We're unable to raise voice with him. Would he please go to high gain. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. I'll have him go to high gain. It's probably the glycol pump you hear in the background, and I'm up to the point where I turn on the IMU. Would you recommend I hold off here for a few minutes or go ahead and power up the IMU? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Stand by.

speaker: LMP
text: Hey, get your high gain to working.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston.

speaker: CC
text: Eagle, this is Houston. You can turn on the IMU. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, this is Columbia.

speaker: CC
text: Columbia, this is Houston. Do you read? Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston ...

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Eagle. This is Houston. We've got a noisy downlink on the downvoice backup. Would you please select S band voice to VOICE? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Columbia, this is Houston. Do you read? Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Columbia. Reading you loud and clear. How me?

speaker: CC
text: Roger. About three by, Mike. We've got a lot of noise in the background. It's clearing up now. Break. Eagle, Houston. Do you read? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Eagle. About four by four. Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Just getting a voice check. Say the page you're on in the activation checklist. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. I'm on page 27. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Understand 27. We copy. Out.

speaker: CC
text: Columbia, this is Houston. Would you please give us P00 in ACCEPT. We have a state vector for you. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Stand by one.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Columbia. You have P00 in ACCEPT, and how are you reading me now?

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Understand, we have P00 in ACCEPT. You're about three by in - on the voice, Mike. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. You're coming in loud and clear, and I'm configured for normal voice. If you've got any switch changes, let me know.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We've got some noise somewhere in the system down here, I think. We're working on it. And I've got a 130 landmark update for you, and also a DAP load whenever you're ready to copy. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Stand by one.

speaker: CMP
text: Go ahead with the 130 update.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Mike. Coming at you with the 130, P1 is 98 37 35, P2 98 42 44, 4 miles north. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. P1 98 37 35, P2 98 42 44, 4 miles north of track; and go ahead with your DAP load.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. CSM weight 36651, LM weight 33627, pitch trim minus 0.72, yaw trim plus 0.51. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Both are good readbacks. Out.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Eagle. Are you satisfied with the LGC self test? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Understand. You passed the LGC self test. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Negative. I was asking you if you were satisfied with it. As far as I can tell, it's satisfactory. And also the primary EVAP flow is actuated to number 1 at 96 05. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Copy on the primary EVAP. We've got the low bit rate, Buzz. We couldn't see that LGC self test. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Columbia. The docking tunnel index angle remains unchanged.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Copy. Out.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Eagle is going to secondary transmitter/receiver and secondary power amplifier, and I'll check with you in 60 seconds. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Stand by. We're standing by. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: Columbia, Houston. We are through with the computer. You can go back to BLOCK. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Eagle. On secondary transmitter/receiver and power amplifier, how do you read? Over. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Reading you five by, Buzz. How me? 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. Out.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. That's about the same as before. Switching back to PRIMARY.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Eagle. Back on PRIMARY, and I'm ready to proceed with the steerable antenna activation.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We're standing by, Buzz. Go ahead. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: And I'll go to BIOMED left - right momentarily.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Eagle. Got a real nice lock on - lockon on the steerable antenna, and you should be receiving BIOMED right and PCM high. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Eagle. We got you five by. It's really beautiful. We've got the high bit rate and the BIOMED. Out.

speaker: CC
text: Eagle, Houston. Do you copy? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Copy.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Eagle. For your information, we're doing the glycol pump check now.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Copy.

speaker: LMP
text: And there's the secondary glycol pump.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: And I'm on secondary, or number 2 pump right now, and I'll hold here for a couple of seconds and then switch back to number 1.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Columbia, Houston. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Columbia. We noticed your DAP configuration. We'd like you to turn off B3 and C4, Mike, and for register 2 in the DAP, we'd like all ones. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: B3 and C4 are both off on panel 8 and I understand you want - Say again what you want on register 2.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. In the DAP, we'd like you load all ones. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: All right.

speaker: CC
text: Columbia, Houston. Did you hit the COMMAND RESET around - after LOS on the last pass? Over.

speaker: CMP
text: That's affirmative. When we were having difficulty getting you, Charlie, I pushed the COMMAND RESET to make sure I had control of high gain.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Thank you much. We're in good shape now. Over.

text: Roger, Tranquility. We copy you on the ground. You got a bunch of guys about to turn blue. We're breathing again. Thanks a lot.

speaker: CDR
text: Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: You're looking good here.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. We're going to be busy for a minute.

speaker: LMP
text: MASTER ARM, ON. Take care of the ... I'll get this ...

speaker: LMP
text: Very smooth touchdown.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. It looks like we're venting the oxidizer now.

speaker: CC

speaker: CC

text: ... circuit breaker.

text: Roger - -

speaker: CC
text: - - We read you five by, Columbia. He has landed, Tranquility Base. Eagle is at Tranquility. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Yes. I heard the whole thing.

speaker: CC
text: ... good show.

speaker: CMP
text: Fantastic.

speaker: LMP
text: Engine STOP RESET.

speaker: LMP

speaker: CC
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: LMP
text: Like - AGS to PGNS align.

speaker: CC
text: Say again?

speaker: LMP
text: Like an AGS to PNGS align. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We're standing by for it.

speaker: LMP
text: ... quantity ...

speaker: CC
text: Eagle, Houston. You are STAY for T2. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Correction, you're - -

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. STAY for T2. We thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, sir.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility Base, Houston. We recommend you exit P12. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Hey, Houston, that may have seemed like a very long final phase. The AUTO targeting was taking us right into a football field size - football field sized crater, with a large number of big boulders and rocks for about ... one or two crater diameters around it, and it required a ... in P66 and flying manually over the rock field to find a reasonably good area.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy. It was beautiful from here, Tranquility. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: We'll get to the details of what's around here, but it looks like a collection of just about every variety of shape, angularity, granularity, about every variety of rock you could find. The colors - Well, it varies pretty much depending on how you're looking relative to the zerophase point. There doesn't appear to be too much of a general color at all. However, it looks as though some of the rocks and boulders, of which there are quite a few in the near area, it looks as though they're going to have some interesting colors to them. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Copy. Sounds good to us, Tranquility. We'll let you press on through the simulated countdown, and we'll talk to you later. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. This one sixth g is just like the airplane.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Tranquility. Be advised there's lots of smiling faces in this room and all over the world. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Well, there are two of them up here.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. That was a beautiful job, you guys.

speaker: CMP
text: And don't forget one in the command module.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. We have you pitched up about 4 1/2 degrees. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: That's confirmed by our local observation.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: And thanks for putting me on relay, Houston. I was missing all the action.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We'll enable MSFN relay.

speaker: CMP
text: I just got it, I think.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Columbia. This is Houston. Say something. They ought to be able to hear you. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger, Tranquility Base. It sure sounded great from up here. You guys did a fantastic job.

speaker: CDR
text: Thank you. Just keep that orbiting base ready for us up there now.

speaker: CMP
text: Will do.

speaker: CC
text: Columbia, Houston. LOS 103 27, AOS 104 13. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility Base, Houston. All your consumables are solid. You're looking good in every respect. We copy the DPS are venting. Everything is copasetic. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Thank you, Houston.

speaker: CDR
text: Houston, the guys that said that we wouldn't be able to tell precisely where we are are the winners today. We were a little busy worrying about program alarms and things like that in the part of the descent where we would normally be picking out our landing spot; and aside from a good look at several of the craters we came over in the final descent, I haven't been able to pick out the things on the horizon as a reference as yet.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Tranquility. No sweat. We'll figure out - We'll figure it out. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: You might be interested to know that I don't think we notice any difficulty at all in adapting to one sixth g. It seems immediately natural to move in this environment.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Tranquility. We copy. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: The area out the left hand window is a relatively level plain cratered with a fairly large number of craters of the 5 to 50 foot variety, and some ridges - small, 20, 30 feet high, I would guess, and literally thousands of little 1 and 2 foot craters around the area. We see some angular blocks out several hundred feet in front of us that are probably 2 feet in size and have angular edges. There is a hill in view, just about on the ground track ahead of us. Difficult to estimate, but might be a half a mile or a mile.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Tranquility. We copy Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Sounds like it looks a lot better than it did yesterday - -

speaker: CMP
text: - - at that very low Sun angle. It looked rough as a cob then.

speaker: CDR
text: It really was rough, Mike. Over the targeted landing area, it was extremely rough, cratered, and large numbers of rocks that were probably some, many larger than 5 or 10 feet in size.

speaker: CMP
text: When in doubt, land long.

speaker: CDR
text: So we did.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. After you get through this P57, we'd like an E memory dump. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. After this first P57, you want an E memory dump.

speaker: CC
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: CC
text: Columbia, Houston. We have a P22 update for you, if you're ready to copy. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: At your service, sir.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Mike. T1, 104 32 18; T2, 104 37 28. And that is 4 miles south. This is based on a targeted landing site. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Roger. Understand based on a targeted landing site; T1, 104 32 18; T2, 104 37 28, and 4 miles south.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CMP
text: Do you have any idea whether they landed left or right of center line? Just a little bit long, is that all we know?

speaker: CC
text: Apparently that's about all we can tell. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston - -

speaker: CDR
text: And, Houston, our mission timer is now reading 902 34 47 and static.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Copy your mission timer's now static. It - Say again the time?

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Copy, Tranquility. That gravity align looked good to us. We see you recycling.

speaker: LMP
text: Well, no. I was trying to get time, 16 65 out, and somehow it proceeded on to the 622 before I could do a VERB 32 ENTER. I want to log a time here, and then I'd like to know whether you want me to proceed on the torquing angles or to go back and reenter again before torquing. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Buzz. Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. We'd like you to recall P57 and run through the gravity align one more time. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. I concur with that.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Tranquility. For the mission timer, two suggestions. Set the circuit breaker, panel 11; also reset and attempt to start. That nine in the first digit might have something to do with it. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. We've tried both of those. If the circuit breaker is in when I reset the - put it in RESET, I get 902 04 40. When I release it now, I get 902 04 49. I'm going to cycle the circuit breaker.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CDR
text: I cycled the circuit breaker and got all nines. And we'll not now reset from all nines.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. We'll research this problem and be back with you momentarily on the mission event time - correction, the mission timer.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay.

speaker: CDR
text: I'd say the color of the - The local surface is very comparable to that we observed from orbit at this Sun angle, about 10 degrees Sun angle, or that nature. It's pretty much without color. It's gray, and it's a very white, chalky gray, as you look into the zero phase line; and it's considerably darker gray, more like a ash - ashen gray as you look out 90 degrees to the Sun. The - Some of the surface rocks in close here that have been fractured or disturbed by the rocket engine plume are coated with this light gray on the outside; but where they've been broken, they display a dark - very dark gray interior; and it looks like it could be country basalt.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Tranquility. We see the NOUN 93, VERB 34.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. I assume you wanted it. Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. Please vent fuel and OX again. Over. It's building back up.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. OX going now.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. You can open both fuel and OX vent now. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Tranquility standing by for GO on a AGS to PGNS align and a lunar align. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. You are GO for the AGS to PGNS align and a lunar align. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. Please vent the fuel. It's increasing rapidly. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: We show 30 psi in the fuel and 30 in the oxidizer.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We're reading somewhat different than that. Stand by.

speaker: CDR
text: The fuel temperature is reading 64 in the descent, and the oxidizer - that's descent 2 - and the oxidizer is off scale low. Descent 1 is showing 61 in the fuel and 65 in the oxidizer.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Stand by. Tranquility, Houston. Please take the fuel vent switch and hold it open. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. We're holding it open. Indicating about 24 psi on board.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CDR
text: Now indicating 20 psi in the fuel side.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CDR
text: And 22 in the OX.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: Now indicating 15 psi in both tanks.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. If you haven't done so, you can release the fuel vent switch now. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. We have indication that we've frozen up the descent fuel helium heat exchanger, and there's some fuel trapped in the line between there and the valvs; and the pressure we're looking at is increasing there. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. Understand.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility Base, Houston. If you have not done so, please close both fuel and OX vents now. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: They're closed.

speaker: CC
text: Thank you, sir.

speaker: CDR
text: From the surface, we could not see any stars out the window; but out my overhead hatch, I'm looking at the Earth. It's big and bright and beautiful. Buzz is going to give a try at seeing some stars through the optics.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Tranquility. We understand. Must be a beautiful sight. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Columbia, Houston. Two minutes to LOS. You're looking great going over the hill. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Thank you. Glad to hear the system's looking good. You have a suggested attitude for me? This one here seems all right.

speaker: CC
text: Stand by.

speaker: CMP
text: Let me know when it's lunch time, will you?

speaker: CC
text: Say again.

speaker: CMP
text: Oh, disregard.

speaker: CC
text: Columbia, Houston. You got a good attitude right there.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility Base, Houston. If you want me to, I can give you a hack on the mission time, every 30 minutes. Over.

speaker: LMP

speaker: CC
text: Roger. You want it counting up? Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. On my Mark, 62 30.

text: MARK.

speaker: CC
text: 62 30 from - past PDI.

text: What we're looking for, Charlie, is the time counting up to T2 that'll be equal to 60 minutes - or T3, be equal to 60 minutes on T3.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We'll have it for you.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility Base, Houston. Reset the event timer to zero and on my Mark at 103 39 41. We'll give you a hack, and it'll be 1 hour. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: And we've got about - almost 3 minutes to go, Neil. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility Base, stand by on the event timer.

speaker: CC

speaker: CC

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. We got it; thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Neil.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. We see the star angle difference. Looks good.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. That last star was Navi, and it wasn't too well distinguishable. I can see where that error could come in. I think for the gravity alignment with one star, Rigel will be quite good.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Stand by on the NOUN 93.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Tranquility Base. Houston. We'd like you to torque that. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Houston, this is Tranquility. Do you want us to accept this position? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. We're looking at it. Stand by. We'd like you to pull the circuit breaker on panel 11 for the mission timer. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. I've already done that, Charlie.

speaker: CC
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. We'd like you to reject that RLS. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: And, Tranquility Base, Houston. We'd like you to call - after this, call P00, and give us a E memory dump.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. Here comes the E memory dump.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: And we got 1106.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Tranquility Base. Houston. Did I copy PROGRAM ALARM 1106 from you? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. That' s affirmative.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. Stand by.

speaker: LMP
text: Could that, by any chance, be due to the fact that I flashed the updata link switch to DATA while that was going on? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Tranquility Base. Houston. The SPAN guys think that's conceivable. Stand by. I think we want another VERB 74.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. Standing by.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Tranquility Base. Houston. We'd like another VERB 74. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Here it comes.

speaker: CC

speaker: CC
text: MARK.

speaker: CC
text: 103 53 - correction, 54.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Tranquility. Houston. We have the LM ascent PAD. If'you're ready to go. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Stand by.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Ready to copy the LM ascent PAD.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Tranquility. TIG, 104 39 47 00, 55358 00322, plus 0022. DEDA 47, plus 37130, minus 70615, plus 58620, plus 56936. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. LM ascent PAD: 104 39 47 00, 55358 00322, plus 0022, plus 37130, minus 70615, plus 58620, plus 56936. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Tranquility. Good readback. We also have a CSI PAD if you are ready to copy.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. We are ready to go.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Coming at you with a CSI: NOUN 11, 105 35 3700, 107 11 3000, 0538, minus all zeros. FDAI is NA, 0937 - correction, 09356, 10315, plus 0538, minus all zeros, plus 0012. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Say again R1 and NOUN 86.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. R1 is plus 0538, and we have a load for you. Will you please give us P00 and DATA? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Before I do that I would like to designate the rendezvous radar up to plus-X.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. CSI readback: NOUN 11, 105 35 3700, 107 11 3000, 0538, minus all zeros, NA, 09356, 10315. NOUN 86, plus 0538, plus all zeros, and the last one was 0012. And what's the sign of that, please?

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. The DELTA-VY is minus all zeros. The DELTA-VZ is plus 0012. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Plus 0012.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Good readback.

speaker: CDR
text: Houston, Tranquility Base. The DSKY's yours, and updata link to DATA.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Thank you, Tranquility.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Tranquility Base. Houston. On my Mark it will be 37 minutes to T3. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: MARK.

speaker: CC
text: Thirty seven minutes till T3.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, this is Houston. It's your computer. We got the load in. You can start your P57.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. Thank you.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Tranquility Base. Does somebody down there have a mike button keyed? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Stand by, and we'll check.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. Do you still hear it now? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: I still hear it. it sounds like somebody banging chairs around in the back room.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. That's a VOGAA that you hear for the CSM to keep the noise down on the loop. Maybe we got a MSFN relay or something. Stand by.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. We got the MSFN relay in. You're hearing the VOGAA, which is a noise suppression device. We'll try to take it out. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: All right. Thank you.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. It ought to be a little quieter up there now. We disabled the MSFN relay.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay. I think the noise has stopped now. Thank you, Charlie.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility Base, Houston. On my Mark, 25 minutes till T3. Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: MARK.

speaker: CC
text: Twenty five minutes until T3.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. Thank you, Charlie.

speaker: CMP
text: Houston, Columbia. How's it going?

speaker: CC
text: Columbia, Houston. We're reading you about three by. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. I'm on OMNI Charlie. How's it going?

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Understand. 0MNI Charlie. Mike, be advised we have an update for you on the P22 for the LM. We estimate he landed about 4 miles downrange. Your T1 times are updated and your T2, if you're ready to copy. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Ready to copy.

speaker: CMP
text: Ready to copy.

speaker: CC
text: Okay. Roger, Columbia. T1 104 32 24, 104 37 33, 2 miles south. Time of closest approach is 104 39 08.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Tranquility Base. Houston. We copy the NOUN 93. You can torque them. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: You said 4 miles long, is that correct, Houston?

speaker: CC
text: That's affirmative, Columbia. It's about 4 miles long. Stand by. We'll have you a map location momentarily. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Houston, Tranquility Base. Do you have an updated LM weight for us? Over.

speaker: CC
text: That's affirmative. Stand by on the DAP. Our DAP PAD for you is LM weight 10906. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. 10906.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Columbia, Houston. With a latitude/longitude over two update for LM position. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Columbia, Houston. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Mike. We got an update on the LAT longitude for the LM, if you're ready to copy. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Go ahead.

speaker: CMP
text: Go ahead.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Columbia, it's plus 7 - correction, plus 0.799 for the LAT, plus 11.730 for the longitude over two. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Thank you. The altitude remain unchanged?

speaker: CC
text: Say again. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Does the altitude remain unchanged? ...

speaker: CC
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Tranquility Base. Houston. You are stay for a T3. We have some surface block data if you're ready to copy. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. Understand we're stay for T3. Stand by.

speaker: CDR
text: Okay, Houston. Go ahead with your block data.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Tranquility. Stand by one.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. Say again your T4 copy. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Correction on T4: 106 38 02. Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Columbia. Houston. We will not come up on the MSFN relay. We'd like you to come on panel 9, turn on your VHF to TR. Over.

speaker: CMP
text: Okay. I'm on panel 9. Ready to receive. You want me to transmit for some reason with it?

speaker: CC
text: Say again, Mike. You're about two by.

speaker: CMP
text: Roger. Panel 9 is configured VHF, RECEIVE. You want me to transmit with the HF for some reason? Why do you want me in TR?

speaker: CC
text: Columbia, this is Houston. We don't want you to transmit, Mike. We just want you in that position in case you want to talk to Tranquility. Break. Tranquility, Houston. Say again. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. I have a fairly good sized difference between battery volts on 5 and 6; 6 is reading 33.5 and 5 is reading 36.5. Is that what you expect? Over.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Stand by.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility, Houston. They are both coming up in voltage. No problem. We're still GO. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Tranquility Base. Houston. Could you please give us a readout now of all of your descent tank pressures? Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Okay, Houston. On descent 1, fuel and oxidizer are reading 10 psi; and descent 2, fuel is reading 10 psi, oxidizer 11 psi.

speaker: CC
text: Roger, Tranquility. Thank you much. Out.

speaker: CDR
text: Houston, Tranquility Base is ready to go through the powerdown and terminate the simulated countdown.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. Standby.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Tranquility Base. Houston. You can start your powerdown now. Over.

speaker: CDR
text: Roger. It's in progress.

speaker: CC
text: And, Tranquility Base, the White Team is going off now and letting the Maroon Team take over. We appreciate the great show. It was a beautiful Job, you guys.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Couldn't of had better agreement from all of you back there.

speaker: LMP
text: Houston, Tranquility.

speaker: CC
text: Go, Tranquility. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Our recommendation at this point is planning an EVA with your concurrence starting about eight o'clock this evening, Houston time. That is about 3 hours from now.

speaker: CC
text: Stand by.

speaker: LMP
text: Well, we will give you some time to think about that.

speaker: CC
text: Tranquility Base, Houston. We thought about it; we will support it. You're GO at that time. Over.

speaker: LMP
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: You guys are getting prime time TV there.

speaker: CDR
text: Hope that little TV set works, but we'll see.

speaker: CC
text: Roger.

speaker: CC
text: Hello, Tranquility Base. Houston. Was your eight o'clock Houston time a reference to opening the hatch or starting the PREP for EVA at that time? Over.

speaker: CDR
text: That would be hatch opening.

speaker: CC
text: That's what we thought. Thank you much.

speaker: CDR

text: Roger. Coming open.

speaker: CC
text: Roger. We copy. Stand by please.

speaker: CC

speaker: LMP
text: Roger. Copy.

speaker: CC

speaker: LMP

speaker: CC
text: Roger. 09018.

speaker: CC
